utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. President. This is case IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I'd like to welcome all those present, Mr. Scott and his assistant, the Defence counsel, the accused, and all the other people in the courtroom. I'm going to start off by giving the floor to the registrar for the IC numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Several parties have submitted lists of documents to be tendered through Witness CV. The list submitted by the OTP shall be given Exhibit number IC 240. The list submitted by 2D will be given comb number IC 241. The list submitted by 3D shall be given Exhibit number IC 242. The list submitted by 4D shall be given Exhibit number IC 243. The list submitted by 5D shall be given Exhibit number IC 244. The OTP has also submitted a list of documents to be tendered through Witness CW. That will be given Exhibit number IC 245. And the OTP has also submitted a list of documents to be tendered through Witness CX. That list will be given Exhibit number IC 246. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I have two oral decisions for today. The first regarding the translation of Exhibit P 02291. During the testimony of Witness BJ on the 29th of August, 2006, at page 5673 of the transcript in French, Counsel Ibrisimovic asked for a new translation of Exhibit P 02291. It concerns a passage in the translation which reads as follows, and I quote: "On the part of the HVO, Mr. Berislav Pusic is appointed liaison officer with UNPROFOR." This exhibit was admitted on the 28th of September, 2006. The registrar has informed us that the CLSS, the translation service, provided a new translation that was requested, and therefore I request that the registrar in these proceedings replace the translation that has been admitted by the revised version. Second oral decision concerning the expert report by Mr. Patrick van der Weijden. I see that the name hasn't been introduced into the transcript v-a-n d-e-r and then W-e-i-j-d-e-n, Weijden. On the 15th of December, 2006, the Prosecution submitted to the Defence and the Chamber the expert report by Mr. Patrick van der Weijden pursuant to Article 94 bis of the Rules of Procedure. In their response dated the 15th of January, 2007, the Defence teams of the six accused challenged the admission of this report contesting the quality of the expert in matters of ballistic science. However, the Defence did not contest the qualifications of this expert with regard to isolated shots or the relevance of this report, reserving the right to further challenge the probative value of seven aspects of his report. They also requested to be able to cross-examine Mr. van der Weijden. The Chamber, having deliberated on the expert report would like to emphasise first of all that the Defence teams have not provided a single specific reason to justify their opposition to the request filed by the Prosecution on the 15th of December, 2006. Furthermore, having read the expert report and the curriculum vitae of its author, the Chamber considers that Mr. Patrick van der Weijden is well used to giving testimony as an expert witness concerning the subjects he deals with in his report. More specifically, isolated firing techniques and shots. In response to a request from the Defence the Chamber conscious that Mr. Patrick van der Weijden should testify in person before the Tribunal in order to answer questions from the Defence teams during the cross-examination. This will allow counsel to challenge the credibility of the conclusions reached in the expert report. The Chamber is of the opinion that only after hearing the examination and cross-examination of Mr. Patrick van der Weijden will it be able to determine definitely the probative value of the expert report. In view of the highly technical report of this expert report, the expert witness shall be granted permission to consult the report while giving testimony in order to explain the conclusions arrived there. The Chamber accords two hours for the examination-in-chief and three -- four hours -- and four hours for the cross-examination, giving each Defence team 40 minutes unless the Defence teams decide to divide up the time amongst themselves differently. And in order to summarise, the expert witness will have his report in front of him when he testifies. The Prosecution will have a maximum of two hours to ask him questions, and the Defence will have four hours in total to cross-examine the expert witness. Each of the counsel has 40 minutes at their disposal unless regulated otherwise by the Defence teams. So those are the rulings for today, and this latter ruling for the expert witness. Pursuant to our request, three days before the expert witness comes in we will hear victim witnesses who will come in to testify, that is to say on the 31st of January and the beginning of February and the 5th of February, and the expert witness will be coming in on the 6th, 7th, and 8th of February. Now, there is a third point that I would like to make pursuant to Mr. Karnavas's request to be given 20 minutes for a 65 ter meeting. The Chamber has not yet deliberated on the grounds for that request, but with respect to the 20 minutes, we will have to find the time to have this meeting either -- if this witness finishes perhaps at 6.30 or 20 to 7.00 and then I will grant Mr. Karnavas 20 minutes. If we have not finished with this witness by then the Defence will be given 20 minutes tomorrow during which to put forward their opinions. If I understood Mr. Karnavas, Mr. Karnavas would like to intervene pursuant to a request made by the Prosecution with regard to 92 bis (A) and (B) of the Rules of Procedure regarding a filing concerning Gornji Vakuf, and the Defence filed a response on the 12th of January, 2007, as far as I can see, and the Prosecution responded to that on the 18th of January, 2007. So I think, Mr. Karnavas, that you're going to want to raise the issue of the response you received with special reference to the last paragraph of the document. So we're going to devote 20 minutes either at the end of today's proceedings or at the beginning of tomorrow's session to discuss the issue. From my point of view, what you want to say has to do with the response that you have received from the Prosecution; is that right? Because I am wary of the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President; good afternoon, Your Honours. It's the reply to our response. The leave to reply which was also the reply, there are some contents in that reply which we believe need to be addressed, certain issues that were raised by the Prosecution which I think deserve to be heard both by the Defence and by the Prosecution. I don't want to elaborate on that. Incidentally, I believe, prior to coming here today, to our commencement of the proceedings, there was a filing to at least give the Trial Chamber an update as to the general issues that we wanted to address. So you'll have that in writing. You should have that, at least. It was filed. It was filed before we started here today. Also just with -- since I'm on my feet, with respect to the sniper expert, just to inform the Trial Chamber we did make a request to meet with the gentleman prior to him testifying. The Prosecution agreed and has made -- is making the gentleman available. We want to thank the Prosecution for making that arrangement, and we want to express this on the record to show you that the Prosecution is assisting us and we're working to expedite that -- that witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Just a moment, please. What you've just said, the Judges are going to deliberate tomorrow because this is the first time that this has been brought up before this Trial Chamber, to know whether the Defence can meet with a Prosecution witness before the proceedings. So this is a question of principle that we're going to have to deal with, confer, and deliberate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't think -- you need to deliberate on that. The Prosecution has agreed to allow us to meet with the expert witness. They can be present, and in fact I believe they will be present. It's merely to -- to discuss with them what exactly they did, because the report we received is not comprehensive as one would expect from an expert of this nature. So I don't think that there's -- that the Prosecution is going to be prejudiced. They will be present. Of course, we will do answer instructed, but I think -- I must say it is common practice, at least in the adversarial procedures, to be -- to have access to the expert witness provided that you either monitor the meeting or, you know, it's done in the presence of the other party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll let you know tomorrow in the afternoon. We'll tell you what we have decided on this matter. And once a witness takes the solemn declaration, he is no longer a witness of either party but of justice. Let us have the next witness brought in. As to duration, we have decided to give the Prosecution one and a half hours and to give the Defence one and a half hours as well, plus the Judges' questions, which I'm sure will be forthcoming, which will allows us to conclude with this witness and might provide us with the 20 minutes we need for the Defence to be able to develop their arguments.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I -- may I, thank you, Your Honour. May I say something about that allocation? It just happens that the Petkovic Defence are first off on this particular witness, but it's this, Your Honour, that the standard guidelines and practice adopted, which are reflected in what Your Honour has just said, we submit, really don't work very well for a witness of this nature, because the result is, we're talking about 15 minutes each in fact, nobody really has enough to do a proper cross-examination and, Your Honour, you can see from yesterday's examination of a witness that we are very economical and we don't explore issues unnecessarily, but, for example, Ms. Alaburic and I, we discussed the cross-examination. From Mr. Petkovic's point of view there is really no way that 15 minutes is enough. I'm not seeking an hour or anything like that, Your Honour, but 15 minutes isn't enough. And Mr. Petkovic -- there are two things. First of all, he is with respect to entitled to sufficient time for his counsel to cross-examine. On the other hand, he's not entitled to have time from our colleagues. And I should say that among the Defence teams we all enjoy excellent personal and professional relations, but we're not entitled --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stewart, I hear what you're saying, but what you're telling us now was discussed before you arrived. Mr. Stewart, at the beginning the Prosecution told us that they needed three years to present their case, three years. Now, if you make the calculations mathematical, if the Defence would need the same time then that means the trial would last 21 years for six accused. So that's the general framework. And you're telling us that you need a lot of time to examine the journalist that is arriving.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I didn't quite say that, with respect, Your Honour. I said that 15 minutes was unnecessarily tight. And, Your Honour, the overall timetable relates to the point that I alluded to, that yesterday we were very economical. Some witnesses we don't use and we won't need to use the time, but some witnesses simply don't lend themselves to the cross-examination for any one client being adequately covered in 15 minutes. I'm not asking for a lot of time, Your Honour, but what I am asking is for -- and we haven't heard the evidence from the witness yet, he's in court now, but I'm just asking for a little flexible when we come to it, Your Honour, when we can get a feel of it, but my prediction -- perhaps I'll be completely wrong but my prediction, Your Honour, is that at 15 minutes it will not have been possible to cover the ground. I should be as quick as I can. I put down that marker. I make that request, Your Honour. May I -- well, I can renew it of course but perhaps, Your Honour, I can simply renew it in the light of where we are in a couple of hours' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have heard what you said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you stand, please, sir. Before you take the solemn declaration, for the transcript would you please give me your first name, last name, and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Jeremy Bowen, 6th of February, 1960.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what is your present occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm journalist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm -- I work for the BBC. I'm the Middle East editor for the BBC.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, have you ever testified before in front of a court on the events that took place in Bosnia-Herzegovina in the years 1990 to 1993, 1994, or is this the first time that you're testifying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it's not the first time. I testified in the trial of Tuta and Stela.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you were a Prosecution witness or a Defence witness in that trial?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was a Prosecution witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. How long did you testify in the Tuta Stela trial?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was a few years ago. I can't remember exactly, but I was there, I think, for most of one day. There was a break for lunch. I was there in the morning and in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And the cross-examination took place on the same day after the Prosecution's examination-in-chief, I assume?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was all done in one day. The whole -- my whole testimony was in the course of a single day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Thank you for explaining that to us. It might be useful to the two parties. Would you now read the solemn declaration, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. You may be seated. I'm just going to give you some information about the proceedings. The Prosecution will have an hour and a half for the examination-in-chief, and the Defence will also have one and a half hours. Now, as opposed to the Tuta and Stela trial, we have six accused and 12 counsel, and you might be asked questions by the accused as well in addition to their Defence counsel. The Bench will also be asking you questions, I'm sure. So the Judges can ask questions as well. As I've just said, I know I will and I assume my colleagues will too. When you give your answers try and be as precise as possible and as brief as possible and answer the question asked. If you have trouble understanding a question, don't hesitate for the person asking the question to restate it. During the examination-in-chief, you might be shown documents by the Prosecution and a video which was broadcast by the BBC. So I'm sure we're going to see the fruits of your labours. Having said that, I give the floor to Mr. Scott who has an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon Mr. President, Your Honours, and to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Bowen.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, the Judge has taken you through already very briefly some of your background. Just very quickly again, is it correct, sir, that you were born in Cardiff on the 6th of February, 1960?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you are and have been for some years a journalist with the BBC?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yeah, almost 23 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that you joined the BBC in 1984, spent the first two years in London completing your BBC training?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell us a bit more about how you are currently assigned?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: My job at the moment, the job I've had for about 18 months is the Middle East editor of the BBC. That means I'm the main on-air person commenting and analysing the Middle East on -- on BBC news. I live in London but I travel very frequently to the region.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Sir, leading up to your time in Mostar that you're going to tell us about today, I'd like to ask you just a bit more about your background. Is it correct, sir, that between approximately -- for approximately seven or eight years beginning in 1987 you were a foreign correspondent first based in Geneva and later based in London?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In the course of that time, sir, is it correct that you reported on approximately -- stories in approximately 60 countries involving a number of armed conflict situations around the world?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes. In that period between 1987 and the mid 1990s I essentially went to all the big stories that were going.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that in 1989 you reported on the conflicts, for example, in El Salvador and in Afghanistan?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In late 1989 and early 1990, did you cover the revolution in Romania?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In 1991 did you cover what we I guess describe today as the first Gulf War?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes. I was in -- I was in Baghdad during the period of the war itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you also report from Somalia during the civil war there in 1991?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes and also just before that period I was in China in the martial law period after Tiananmen Square, and that was a big story.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that when you first received your assignments to go to the former Yugoslavia you had a number of years of experience not only reporting on foreign stories but specifically armed conflict situations?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yeah. When I first went to former Yugoslavia in 1991 I was 31 years old and I'd say that of my generation I was about the most experienced reporter the BBC had at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So I'm going to pause and caution both of us perhaps to speak a bit more slowly, mindful of the interpreters, please?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No problem. Sir is it correct that in 1995 while a BBC correspondent in the Middle East, you won an award for -- as the best news correspondent at the New York Television Festival?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In 1996, did you receive an award for best breaking news report concerning the an assassination of Israeli Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you in fact receive an award at the Monte Carlo Film and TV Festival in connection with the documentary "Unfinished Business" which we will look at later today?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That was in 1994?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes, it was, yes. It was awarded in 1994 for work produced in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell us, sir, finally, did you also receive an award in connection with the coverage of the arrest of Saddam Hussein in Iraq?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes, I won a Sony Gold Award.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: With this background, sir, let me turn to your -- particularly your experience in the former Yugoslavia. Can you tell the Judges when you first went to Yugoslavia and on what assignment?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I first went to Yugoslavia in 1991 when the war started in Croatia. I went first of all from Belgrade and went to the -- the Serb enclaves on the Croatian side of the river Danube and then I was based in Zagreb, and I worked extensively on the Croatian side. I was in, among other places, Vukovar, Osijek, and most of the main theatres of warfare during that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Later, as part of your reporting in the former Yugoslavia, did you -- were you based in and report from the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yeah. I first went to Sarajevo in July of 1992, and I went after that pretty constantly until just before the end of the war in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you just briefly describe your work in Sarajevo and the conditions that you reported on while you were there?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Well, during the time I was actually working out of the city of Sarajevo and I worked elsewhere in Bosnia as well, I reported on the siege, on the progress of the war, on the international humanitarian mission. First and foremost, I suppose, the main story for us was the plight of the civilians who were caught up in the siege, actually on both sides of the lines. I also tried to work as much as I could on the Serb side. I also travelled to Eastern Bosnia. I also went to -- from thereafter I went to the Gorazde enclave and I also worked in -- by the, sort of, autumn of 1992, when tension was rising in Central Bosnia, I worked quite a bit in Central Bosnia as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you a few more questions about Sarajevo before moving forward. What was your personal experience there in terms of the shelling and sniping that was going on in that city at that time?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Well, all the -- well, the vast majority of foreign journalists who were in Sarajevo stayed in the Holiday Inn hotel, which was right in the centre of the city and very close to the confrontation line that ran down the middle of the city. So we were right in the centre of the sniping and shooting. You couldn't go out the main door of the hotel because of a sniper. You couldn't stay at the front of the hotel because of sniping and shooting. The hotel itself was quite often hit. So we were -- you know, we experienced the war in all its -- you know, in all its characteristics. Of course, as foreign journalists we were able to get out, which was the big advantage we had over the people who lived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What was the humanitarian situation in Sarajevo during that time?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Well, it was pretty desperate because of the -- the killing. The food situation -- once the crisis at the beginning of the war got out of the way and once the humanitarian airlift started, the food situation was you know contained. People had just about enough to eat. The main problem there was the fact that they -- the vast majority of them anyway couldn't leave and it was very dangerous because there was no place in the city where you couldn't be hit by a shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In the course of your work in Sarajevo, can you tell the Judges, did you visit and report from or about the -- the two principal hospitals there, the Kosovo hospital and the state hospital?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes. Like all the journalists there, I went to those hospitals many times. If you work in a war zone as a journalist, a hospital is quite a good place to try to find stories, to try to talk to victims of war, and if you're lucky, it's a little bit less dangerous than being out on the streets, although, of course, we were out on the streets every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier that you also travelled to and reported from or about the city of Gorazde. Again, can you just by way of back brief background tell us what you experienced in that situation in?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: In August of 1992, the UNHCR and one of their local staff who is called Larry Hollingworth arranged a convoy into Gorazde. Gorazde at that time was -- hadn't had any kind of relief effort since the beginning of the wore. So Larry Hollingworth arranged a number of local cease-fires, he arranged permission to get through Serb territory en route to Gorazde. We went through Rogatica, for example, where we had a few problems but essentially we got through. And then when we arrived in Gorazde, the people were very happy to see us. It was -- I immediately thought of pictures I had seen of towns in Europe being liberated in World War II by the Allied forces. Everyone came rushing out with flowers in their gardens, were overjoyed because they thought they were being rescued; of course, that mission was only there for a day. They were very pale. Although it was a very hot summer they had been indoors the whole time, and you could see the damage in the city. There was a fair amount of war going on there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may interjection there, Your Honour, and I -- excuse me, sir. And I'm certainly -- I'm sure the gentleman has a lot of stories about Bosnia. The work, you know, took place all over the country but given the limited nature of our time, I think we best just focus in on, you know, Sarajevo was fine, but now we can get to Mostar. I just think it's best -- I mean, we're not challenging that the gentleman wasn't there and wasn't aware of what was happening in Gorazde or Srebrenica or other places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Scott, that is just what I was thinking a few moments ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We are almost finished, Your Honour. In fact we are finished with the background.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's true that --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... There --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So having set the stage can we move to the heart of the matter because the witness has enormous experience, and everything that he lived through we could listen to for day, but of course we must go to the heart of the matter, to the essential points which are Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour, he could talk about it for days, and I've just spent a very few minutes giving the Court some background on his experiences especially specifically in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Specifically before we turn to Mostar, sir, you said you'd also gone into the area of Central Bosnia which is indeed related to evidence in this case. Can you tell us what was the occasion -- on what occasion did you go into Central Bosnia and for what purpose, in terms of what reporting were you doing?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I wanted to find out what was happening in Central Bosnia by about I suppose by now we're talking about the autumn of 1992. So I travelled with my team right through the Lasva valley. I went to it all the main places there, all the main towns, and I also -- one of the -- I also started to get some direct experience of Bosnian Croat ideas through a meeting I had in Busovaca with Dario Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: How did you come to meet and interview Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Through the -- our local fixer, translator, who was a woman from Zagreb who had had some connection with him. I'm not quite sure what it was. But she said, "Look, this is a guy," I hadn't heard of him at that point. She said, "This is a guy you really ought to meet because he's very important and he's going to be more important," and essentially what we spoke about was the national project that the Croatians had.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me just back up for a moment did you in fact sit down and meet with Dario Kordic and, if so, where approximately?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: On a hill outside Busovaca. There was -- I think it was a small village, and we went up to this. He had a sort of headquarters. You could call it a war room. There were maps and so on, and he had a small office there. I remember it quite vividly because it had had brown suede wallpaper and in that office we spoke for -- we had quite a long consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You said a few moments ago, and I'm looking at the transcript, that Kordic spoke about the national project that the Croatians had. Can you tell the Judges anything more Mr. Kordic said about that?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I can't give you direct quotes on it because it's a quite a long time ago and I haven't got my notebook with me. But what I can say is that you know he spoke about the kind of fellow feeling they had with Zagreb, the fact that they felt that there was a connection and -- and they also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I notice that the gentleman did not testify in Kordic. Obviously he would have been available at Kordic. Mr. Kordic, you know, was tried, was convicted, and of course he's unavailable to bring in as a witness. I find that we are handicapped in this situation in light of the fact that now, for the first time, we're going into matters which are not detailed, which are not in the gentleman's witness statement that was taken. So I would -- I would -- I would object to going into any detail --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, what is interesting in the statement, there is something that evokes that meeting. You shouldn't say that it would be a prejudice if what he's saying were compared with what Mr. Kordic had to say, and you can always compare that with what Mr. Kordic has said. So you can't say that he cannot testify about that. Mr. Scott, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Just for the record, the Court is absolutely correct. It's on page 2 of the witness's statement. It's very explicit and it's just a completely false statement to say that it wasn't in the witness's prior statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Hold on. Excuse me. I'm going to object to that characterisation that it's -- that it's false.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir, you should know better. Now, there's one sentence here. There's no elaboration. I do not have access to Mr. Kordic nor do I know whether Mr. Kordic testified or not in this trial but he's certainly not available to be cross-examined here. I do -- Mr. Kordic is not part of this trial. The Prosecution could have called the gentleman during -- in the Kordic case if they thought that that was an issue. And so that's why I would -- I would object to the gentleman going into any specific details with respect to his conversation with Mr. Kordic. It does prejudice us because we do not have -- he's unavailable. I understand that hearsay information can come in, but the gentleman -- but the gentleman is unavailable to be cross-examined.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, number one, Your Honour, that's no basis for an objection the an all. It's no basis at all. And if Mr. Karnavas wants to call Mr. Kordic, I assume he can have him brought here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Judges have deliberated. As you know, we react very quickly and we don't need hours to reach our decision. We have deliberated, and we have decided that the Prosecution can ask questions about things that are featured in the statement, in the written statement, because this is what the Defence has been informed about, and the Defence with equally cross-examine on the contents of the statement. Mr. Scott, there are four or five sentences that do feature in the written statement, so you can examine starting from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Really, we were virtually done with it. I just simply ask the witness to tell us as much as he could remember about the conversation with Mr. Kordic about the so-called "national project" involving Croatia and he -- I think his answer was interrupted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So, sir, Mr. Bowen, if you can recall let me just ask you the question again. Can you just tell us as much as you can recall about what Mr. Kordic told you about this national project with Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Well, essentially he was talking -- the theme of his remarks was that the Bosnian Croats had rights, that they wanted to be separate from other people in Bosnia, and -- and the underlying tone of the conversation and the mood of it was they felt quite secure in this because they knew they had the backing of the Tudjman government in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, sir, moving then specifically to Mostar. Can you please tell the Judges, then, as we prepare to look at the video, the documentary that you prepared, how did you first come to know about Mostar and become interested in reporting about that location and things that were happening there?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: There was a briefing every morning at the headquarters of UNPROFOR in Sarajevo for journalists, as well as a military briefing from the UNPROFOR people. There was also after that always a humanitarian briefing from the UNHCR. One morning in -- it would have been late July or early August of 1993, I think early August of 1993, the UNHCR spokesman, who is called Peter Kessler, talked about -- for the first time talked about the situation on the east side of Mostar. I roughly remember him saying that there are I think he said 25.000 people approximately there, very little food, very little water, under siege, surrounded, and he also said that there was -- and he used this phrase: "There was a Ho Chi Minh trail into Mostar from Jablanica." So where they were -- the Bosnian army were bringing in supplies. So as a reporter I immediately thought, well, I want to go down that road. I want to go down that trail. I want to get to Jablanica and get to Mostar to try to find out what's going on there because it was a newish theatre of war, and so it was -- it was clearly going to be an important story.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, I'm going to spend the next few minutes asking you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. Sir, Mr. Bowen, you have just told us -- so far we haven't heard anything like this, you have just told us that every morning UNPROFOR had a briefing for journalists. So we conclude that you were present there. According to your own feelings, you were familiar with the events that we can qualify as very important events. What you saw at the UNPROFOR meetings, did they seem well-informed, objective, or did you have a feeling that their reports were not very accurate? What was your feeling? What would be your sentiment about those press conferences, and who was it who was in charge of those press conferences? Was it the spokesman for UNPROFOR, the commander of UNPROFOR? Who was it who delivered those press conferences?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Generally speaking the press conferences were delivered by the spokespeople for UNPROFOR. At that time I can't remember. It might have been Barry Frewer, who was a Canadian military officer. There were a couple of others too who would speak at different times. I thought in general they were quite reliable on some things. For example, every morning they would give a shell count. The UN military observers would actually count how many shells had exploded in Sarajevo and they'd give us that. That would be interesting. And some other details. I was conscious at that sometimes I felt that they were trying to spin the United Nations line. There was -- for example, there was a controversy that year, I think, about whether or not what was happening in Sarajevo was a siege or what the spokesman called a strategic encirclement. For their own political reasons they didn't want to call it a siege. However. The -- we used to get more material, frankly, out of the UNHCR briefings because they were about civilians, about the plight of civilians, and I generally -- at this it point Peter Kessler, who gave that briefing about Mostar and said that there was this "Ho Chi Minh trail going into Mostar," at this point I knew him for at least a year and I found his information to be reliable. He'd been a good source of stories and very helpful. So I had known Peter -- I knew him. We were on first name terms. We were colleagues really by that stage, and so I spoke to him after the briefing and he gave me a little bit more information, and I had no reason to doubt that he was telling the truth on this. He was also quite -- he was quite exercised about it. You know, he said, "Look, there's a real story down there. There's some people, 25.000 people who are in a lot of trouble," and he said, "We can't get conveys in there. And the only way to get in, as far as we know, is with the Bosnian army through the mountains on foot. And if we want to get convoys in we have to use the roads and at the moment we're not able to get through the Bosnian Croat lines." So in other words, Your Honour, it sounded like a good story and one well worth pursuing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What about this Ho Chi Minh trail? I understand what it is. For the transcript could you please explain what you mean by this Ho Chi Minh trail?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the phrase is a reference to the supply line that the North Vietnamese established to take supplies down to the guerrilla fighters in South Vietnam during the Vietnam war versus the Americans in the 1960s. This was on a much smaller scale, but by Ho Chi Minh trail, what I took it to mean was that there was an overland route on foot away from the roads leading ultimately through the front line and into the besieged sector of Mostar, and you know, to be honest I was very intrigued by it. It sounded like it would be -- even getting there would be a very interesting experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I was about to ask you, I'm going to spend a few minutes now asking you about your two visits or trips into Mostar, and can we just say for now for the record is it correct, sir, that on the basis of these two trips that we're going to talk about, a BBC document was prepared entitled "Unfinished Business"?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. I also did a third visit there in the early part of 1994, but the two -- the documentary that I think you're going to see is based on those two trips in August and September and October of -- of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, following up on the president's questions, can you tell us a bit more then what you did to gain access or go into East Mostar the first time in August 1993?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: It was very complicated. These days if you want to drive from Sarajevo to Mostar it takes about -- I think less than two hours. During the war it took us three days. We first of all had to get permissions to cross various front lines to get out of the city of Sarajevo. We then drove along the -- actually, the main road for a while, the main Sarajevo-Mostar road. Then somewhere near the town of Konjic it was blocked because that's where the war was starting again basically, because up to there between Sarajevo and, there, there was an enclave controlled by the Bosnian government. At that point and by this stage it was sort of beginning to get dark on the first day. We then diverted off to the main road. We were going south, so I guess it would be to the west. Went through some forest tracks. There was a -- quite a thick forest, and there were some narrow tracks, and some soldiers said -- I said, "Jablanica road, where is Jablanica?" And they pointed, "Up there." So basically we had no real idea where we were doing. But we went off through this forest. It got very dark and very late and, in the middle of the forest that night, I saw a light on and we knocked on the door and we stayed there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, sir. During your journey through the forest, did you have flak vests or were you marked as press or were you wearing civilian clothes, just ordinary civilian clothes? How were you dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were wearing civilian clothes. We'd always wear that, but we were travelling in a -- in an armoured Land Rover which was marked BBC, and we also -- we weren't wearing them inside the vehicle, but we also had -- with us inside the vehicle we had flak jackets and helmets me and my colleagues I had three colleagues there with me. In fact, we knew it was very -- we thought it was very -- we heard it was quite dangerous in this forest, so we locked the doors on the inside and then we were trying to have discussions about what do we do if we were stopped by men with guns and we had various strategies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, once you'd reached Jablanica, can you tell us then, just continue the story from -- once you'd reached Jablanica, how did you get to Mostar?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: We reached Jablanica by about the middle of the second day of our journey. We -- I just started asking people questions. I said, "Look," I was -- there's a hotel there in Jablanica. Jablanica is not a very big town. There was a Spanish UN base there, and we went there first of all, and we left the car there and our supplies. They said it was important to because there was no law in Jablanica. It would get stolen otherwise. And we walked then to the hotel. I think it was called the Hotel Bosna but I may be wrong on that. They said that "You should go there and try and meet people who travel between Jablanica and Mostar." And while we were there someone -- I just was asking complete strangers, you know, if they knew how to do this and someone put us in touch with a man called Humo. Humo, it turned out, was -- he described himself as the deputy commander of fighters in the east side of Mostar, and he offered to help us get in. In fact, he said he'd been in Sarajevo and he'd been there to try and find a TV crew to come in with him and he couldn't find one and was returning empty handed. So he was quite pleased to see us. And he told us to come to -- the following morning to a place called Glogosnica. I think that's something like the correct pronunciation which is a just a little ways south of Jablanica, and this place was where they started their -- their convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, can you describe -- well, first of all how long did it take you to then travel by foot from Jablanica to Mostar?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: It took I'd say about 18 or 20 hours. It was a very long day, and quite a bit of the night. We -- they had a -- a caravan of about 20 or 25 pack horses and I think some mules as well. Most of the horses and mules were carrying ammunition, and we rented from them four horse to put our equipment on, and we walked with the horses and -- following the horses and following Humo, we walked till we got there. I mean, there was some delays en route. We were shot at, at one point, and we had to wait there for -- until it got dark, until might fell and it was safe to go on. And we finished the journey the last few miles. What happened was you walked to the outlying villages in the northern part of their enclave, and then they would then -- unloaded the horses, loaded all the ammunition. It amounted to just one truckload. And then we sat on top of it with various Bosnian army soldiers and then drove in from -- from that village into the centre of East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, we need to move on a bit, but let me just ask you before we leave going on the -- going over on the mountain trail, can you just describe for the Judges the nature of this trail? Are we talking about a road? Are we talking about a single footpath can you just describe what this path looked like and consisted of?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: It was a single footpath, very steep in places. I was amazed the horses, some of which were very heavily laden, were able to keep their footing, and from Jablanica there was quite a steep climb up through wooded slopes, and then when you got to the -- the top, there was a big mountainous plateau. There was a plateau surrounded by mountains but open ground by then. And so a lot of the walk was through open ground. I mean, it was -- it's fantastic terrain. You know, it would be a great hike to do in peacetime but over two days. We did it over a day; it was very tough.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could you tell the Judges what your understanding was whether there was anyway into East Mostar other than this mountain trial that you've described?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: My understanding from talking to the -- to Humo especially was that this was the only way in.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is it correct, sir, that you then when you arrived in Mostar you remained in the first occasion, your first visit, for approximately seven to 10 days?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yeah, that's right. Seven to 10 days I think that's about it. Maybe more like 10 than seven.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you just briefly tell us where you stayed during this time when you were actually in town?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I stayed -- I stayed in -- no, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic would like to intervene.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like you to ask the witness whether it was his own wish to use the military trail [phoen], or maybe he could have used the protection of UNPROFOR and go from Jablanica to Mostar along the Neretva valley. I believe that the witness could have chosen to be a protected person and join the UNPROFOR and take the regular road. I believe that he did it of his own will, that he went on this steep trail of his own will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a question that can be asked during cross-examination. However, General Petkovic's question reminds me of another question that I wanted to put to you, sir. Before you left Jablanica, did you inform UNPROFOR that you were headed for Mostar along that trail, and did they maybe tell you it is dangerous. Why don't you come with us? What was the position of UNPROFOR regarding your intention to go on that journey along that particular trail?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say -- first of all, I did tell the UNPROFOR people in Jablanica, the Spanish Battalion who were there, I told them where we were going because I asked them how we could get in and did they know people who could help us. As to whether we could ride with UNPROFOR. Well, it didn't work like that with journalists in Bosnia. I can't think of I can think of a couple of occasions with the British UNPROFOR troops in Central Bosnia, but it was my experience that it was a very, very rare that you were able to travel with UNPROFOR as part of their convoy. Generally speaking they didn't allow that. Sometimes people would try to follow them, but generally what happened was that, if you tried to just follow an UNPROFOR convoy, they'd get to a roadblock, they'd be waved through, and if you tried to follow them you'd be stopped. So we tried that kind of thing around Sarajevo, just following UNPROFOR, and it just -- it didn't work out. Unless you had -- for example, the convoy I went on to Gorazde, that was a UNHCR convoy with UNPROFOR protection, and they incorporated us right in the centre of the convoy, because what always happened with journalists' vehicles was, if you were just following the last APC in the convoy, then whether it was Bosnian army, Serb, or Bosnian Croat roadblocks, you'd always get stopped and you then would be in -- you know, the very -- the best -- the best outcome would be that you would be turned back and the worst outcome would be you'd be in a lot of trouble. So by the summer of 1993 it had been two years that the war in Croatia had started. I'd spent a lot of time there and I'd been through a lot of roadblocks and stopped at a lot and I didn't want to be I thought there would be no future in just following them because the Spanish people didn't say that we could go with them. So therefore that reinforced my feeling that the only way in was with the Bosnian army. I mean, that's the message I also got from the Spaniards which was, you know, that's your way in if you want to do it. Also, I have to say that the Spanish were quite well known for -- they weren't particularly proactive in that area. They did various patrols but they weren't amazingly active. So I felt that -- I also felt, frankly, that it was part of the story to do it with the Bosnian army because that was part of the story, how they got their supplies in. Had it been possible to go with UNPROFOR I don't know which choice I would have made. But anyway, we didn't have the choice. As far as I was concerned, and as far -- that was based on what I was hearing, not least from UNPROFOR, that the only way in was through this trail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Scott, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, I was just asking you just briefly to tell us just so the Judges again have some idea of the conditions you encountered, where did you stay, you your crew, during this first trip to Mostar in August?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: The first night that we arrived in Mostar we stayed at the building - I think it was a former bank - that the Bosnian forces there were using as their HQ. After that, for a few nights we stayed in a cellar opposite the war hospital in Mostar which they fitted out as an overflow hospital ward, but we had to move from that because it was filling up with wounded. So they needed -- they needed the beds that we were occupying. So we made a deal with a man who lived in -- who had a house next door. We basically rented his house for whatever number of Deutschmarks it was and stayed there for the rest of the time. It was just opposite the war hospital, this particular house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the transcript, could you give us the exact date, please? When did you arrive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't -- I'm sorry I can't give you the exact date. Had I noticed that, I might have been able to find it, but I can tell you it was sometime around the second or third week of August, I would say, of 1993. It was about -- it was -- I can tell you more precisely. It was five for six days before the first UNHCR convoy got into Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, just looking ahead at the documentary, the Judges will hear early in the documentary you make the statement that at that time Mostar was the most vicious theatre of fighting in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Can you tell it the Judges how did what you see in Mostar at that time compare to what you'd seen in other parts of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Well, it was really the intensity of it. The only place I saw that -- I mean, I felt I could make a judgement like that because essentially I'd been to all the other theatres of fighting. The only place I'd seen that had been comparable with it was the previous year -- no, two years previously - sorry - in Vukovar. But I used that phrase at the time because as it was there in 1993, it was much more intense. I was comparing it mainly to Sarajevo. I mean, there it was much more intense. It was a smaller area. There wasn't the international dimension there in terms of humanitarian aid. There was a lot of damage. The pressure on the civilian population because of the lack of international aid, because of the smallness of the area, the fact it was pretty crowded with people, all that meant that the people there were under a great deal of pressure and that I also factored into the -- you know, the intensity because modern wars are really about their effect on civilians, to a large degree. Modern wars - and I've seen this all over the world - are fought very much because of the -- the impact on the civilians is a major part of the impact of modern war, and there was a strong impact, a very serious impact on the civilians of East Mostar at that particular time, which I -- you know, I saw immediately really in the first couple of days.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You said a moment ago in reference to a benchmark in time if you will in response to the president's question that you arrived there approximately five or six days before an UNHCR convoy arrived in August 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did -- did you understand that was the first convoy that had actually come into East Mostar for some substantial time?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I will object to the leading nature. I understand it's -- you know, there may be a basis for it, but when we come to this sorts of information, it would be best just to get the information from the witness and not provide the witness with the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us what you knew about this convoy that entered Mostar towards the end of August, 1993?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: What I was told by the UNHCR people who travelled with it, both of whom I'd met at different times, various -- various -- sorry, a number of whom I'd met before was that it was the first convoy that they had got into East Mostar since the fighting had become intense earlier that summer, in the early part of the summer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And -- and where and how were the people living in East Mostar during this time, in terms of what you saw on the first visit?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Well, mainly underground in cellars. There were some quite modern apartment buildings that had big cellars in them. There was a curfew for large parts of the day. The authorities there-one thing that struck me was that it was a very mobilised and quite well organised enclave. The authorities there had a strict rationing system for food. There wasn't a black market like there was in Sarajevo, and most of the people there -- so people got some food but it was very, very little. They had rations of a couple of bowls of soup a day from the authorities. Most people would spend as much time as they could inside and in a cellar, if they had one, because of the -- the dangers of -- of going outside, the dangers coming from sniping and from shelling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bowen, you've just described the situation to us in August, and a witness told us that the first convoy arrived on the 21st of August. So if I understand you correctly, you arrived around the 15th of August. When you arrived, were you the only representative of the international press or did you have other colleagues who were there in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With us was a photographer who had come. She -- we had given her a lift, basically. We had room in the van, in our Land Rover. She was called Alexandra Boulet, and she's a French photographer. There was -- I think -- I'm trying to think. There may have been one person there from the AFP, I think, from the Agence France Presse, and there was someone a few days before just for half a day from CNN but not while we were there. So essentially when we were there we were the only -- certainly the broadcasters who were there and I think -- I can't remember if I saw the man from the AFP in the August trip or the September trip. Maybe it was in September. Anyway, there were very few journalists there. They were all in Sarajevo mainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. Thank you. I asked you the question because in 1990, the international media, when they were in exposed areas there were always live reports. Does that mean in August in Mostar the international media could not report live outside the area about what was going on in town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not live on TV. In those days and things have -- you know, if it was now we could do a live on TV from there because the way -- the equipment these days is much more -- is much smaller, easier to use, it's lighter. These days you can send pictures down a telephone line. But in -- you know, it's 14 years ago. Then to do a TV live you needed probably the best part of a tonne of equipment and big generators, and it just wasn't practical to take it in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You yourself, I assume you had a satellite telephone. Did you call your headquarters in London to tell them that the situation was such-and-such, that it required investment on the part of the media, that is to say to have somebody locally on the ground, that this would be important? Did you communicate with London and explain the situation to them and tell them that the situation was highly specific?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I was going to say, Your Honour, that I did some -- we did have a satellite telephone, and we did some live reports for -- through the satellite telephone, some of which were broadcast on TV and some of which were broadcast on the radio. I certainly said to my people in London it would be great if we could get live TV in there, but at that particular time it was considered too dangerous because it was a very dangerous -- to get at that time, and it's still the case now, but it was absolutely the case then, because of the bulky nature of the equipment and the fact that it would need two engineers to operate it and would be -- the feeling was, it was -- the right decision was that it was too difficult logistically and essentially too dangerous to have that kind of gear in there. You know, it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, there's something that I'm surprised about. You say you had a telephone and that you were in contact with London. But you could have recounted what you were experiencing, and then you have SkyNews or other television changes. You could have the journalist's commentary on a still. So you could say, I'm walking along such-and-such a street. Around me I can see such-and-such. You didn't do anything like that, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Sorry, I obviously didn't explain myself properly. Yes, I did do that kind of thing on the radio, on the telephone, and it was broadcast on the television and also on the radio. In those days satellite phones were -- weighed about 50 kilos so you couldn't walk up and down with them. You had to sit in one place. But we would -- yeah, I certainly used the satellite telephone to do some reports both live and recorded, which I sent out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, after this first trip then in August 1993, you returned to London and what did you do after that in looking forward to the second trip?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: When I got back after that first trip to -- to Mostar, when I got back to London, almost immediately, coincidentally, I was telephoned by a BBC documentary producer called Eamonn Matthews. Eamonn Matthews said to me that he would like to do a documentary with me as the reporter and him as the director and producer about the war in Bosnia. And I said I know exactly where to do this because there's an incredible story there in Mostar, and it's a story that really hasn't been told that much. I'd been a bit -- because of our logistical problems that you've -- that Your Honour mentioned in terms of not having live TV there, I felt that we could have done a much better job with TV. There were many other things we could do. So I was very anxious to go back. So when Eamonn said, "Look we can do this film," I said, "Well, let's go to Mostar. It's the obvious thing to do."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And then what arrangements did you make just logistical arrangements to actually go into East Mostar on this second occasion?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Eamonn, the producer, made the logistical arrangements. He went on a rekkie trip around the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina actually for a week or 10 days, I think, where he looked into other story lines as well. He went to Central Bosnia. He went to Sarajevo. He went to the west side of Mostar. He spoke to the Bosnian Croat authorities. And he didn't go to East Mostar but what he did -- because at that point -- after that first United Nations convoy things opened up a little bit for the -- the international humanitarian effort. So by then it -- it had become possible in the -- in the interim period, it had become possible to cross in by vehicle into -- into the east side of Mostar. So he made an arrangement with the European Monitoring Mission there, the guys in white clothing. He made an arrangement to go -- they said they could get us in and that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And is it correct, sir, that you then returned to East Mostar on the 25th of September, 1993, and stayed on this second occasion approximately two and a half or three weeks?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your documentary shows name of Muslims crossing over or arriving in East Mostar, which we will be seeing in a few minutes. Can you tell the Judges, is that something you saw only once or on a number of occasions?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I saw -- there's one sequence, there's one scene in the film which is filmed at night with a night-vision camera where you see people crossing over the river Neretva. There's gunfire going on as well. They're being shot at -- shot -- gunfire is over their heads, but I could hear the sounds of bullets passing over -- I was with the people and I could hear the sound -- you can also hear on the sound -- track the sound of bullets going over which has a very particular sound you know what it is. So that happened on one particular night. I think it happened on a couple of other nights when we were there but we weren't able to film it. But these were people coming from West Mostar who had been kicked out over the front line. We -- I also saw - on any given day there were small numbers of people milling around looking lost who just arrived. And I remember for example, talking to a pair of sisters, both of whom had babies who had both -- who both said they had come from Capljina, that they'd been badly treated, their husbands had been taken, and -- in fact they said that they thought they had -- they were -- expected to be shot, but they said they thought they'd escaped it because their mother had explained that she was half Croatian, half Croat, and so she felt -- they felt they were then spared. But anyway that was a typical encounter. There were a lot of people who weren't from East Mostar who had come from the surrounding places in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. We have a question from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While you're on this subject, Witness, what you want to say is that when this population, the Muslims, crossed the river Neretva, the civilians, women and children, were the targets of sniping fire were they? Is that what you want to say? Or do you mean that the shots came from the Bosnian Croats targeting the opposite army? Do you understand my question? Were they targeting the people crossing the river or were they targeting the armed forces on the other bank, the opposite bank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were -- it was harassing fire, I felt, because nobody was hit by it, but it was -- the people -- there were women and children and some old men. There were no men of military age. And there was quite a large amount of gunfire, but as I say, nobody was hit. So I think if they had been trying to kill them, they could have done that probably. You know, they could have used mortars as well if they wanted to kill them. I think it was harassment, just to make the experience even more unpleasant, I suppose, because I spoke to quite a few of the people after they came over and they told me -- and it's in the film. They told me some quite hair-raising stories about the experiences that they'd had in the previous few hours as they were thrown out of their homes by forces in West Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're telling us, and this is important for us, you're telling us that the women, children, and the elderly who were crossing the river, that there were shots, but you're saying that if they had wanted to, they could have shot them, hit them. But in fact, that they were -- that it was harassing fire. Is that what you're saying, that this was harassing fire? And I understood it that if they wanted to kill them, to kill these people, they could have used mortars and killed them. So what you saw with your own very own eyes, was it this kind of situation? You saw people crossing and there were shots being fired surround about or above their heads to harass them, to stop them crossing but not with the intention of killing them or wounding them. Would you be very precise on that point, please, and tell us exactly what you think?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My assumption, and it's based on the experience I'd had covering war, and it's not based clearly on talking to the people who were firing, but my assumption was that they were -- it was essentially a terror tactic, that these people had been thoroughly -- as I say, I found out the stories of a lot of them. Not just the people you see on the film. I did a lot of interviews afterwards for two or three hours, and the -- they had been thoroughly terrorised as it was. The male members of their family had been taken away. They assumed or worried that some of them had been killed. They'd been violently expelled from their homes, and my assumption was that the fire directed at them -- I mean, maybe -- I'm assuming that the Bosnian Croat forces were efficient enough to kill them if they wanted to, as I say, by using mortars or by shooting just a little bit lower down. You know, when a bullet goes over your head, it makes a -- it goes -- it makes a "tdzzz" sort of noise, a very characteristic sort of sound, and that's quite close to you. If you hear a bullet making that noises it means the bullet's quite close to you, and so I heard that a lot that night, those bullets were going, you know, very close over our heads. So I guessed that it would have been possible, yeah, if they wanted to have killed them. I think the intention was to terrorise them rather than kill them on that particular night, but, as I say, that was my assumption and not anything I could definitively say. I think that if they wanted to kill them, they probably could have. In fact, they could have killed them before they left West Mostar, if that was the intention.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you've mentioned several times in the last few minutes that the people that you saw coming into East Mostar either from West Mostar or from Capljina that these were women, children, elderly. I think you said a moment ago, you did not see military-aged men; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Of all the people I saw or spoke to coming in from West Mostar or from the surrounding villages, and I saw a lot of people over the period I was there who fit that description. I didn't see any men of military age, and by that I mean there was hardly any even young boys who were able to shave. So it was essentially from beginning of puberty right up to being not strong enough anymore to carry a gun. You know, military age was generally interpreted as something between about 13 and, you know, 65 or 70, frankly, you know, in the case of a fit man of that age.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you gain any knowledge or understanding at that time as to where the Muslim men were, these men of military age?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes. We were told by -- I was told by many different people that they -- by women especially, that their men were in the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you make any effort during the time -- the two times that you were in Mostar in 1993 to visit and film at the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: We tried to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor is moving on to another area, but before he does so, can we go back to your previous answer about the shooting. There were people who were leaving West Mostar and going to East Mostar, and we had this firing, these shots. Now, as far as we Judges are concerned, we would like to know who did the shooting. What would your opinion be? Who did the shooting, shooting round about, shooting up in the air, and harassing fire? Who was it who did the shooting, in opinion, if you know? If you don't know, that's another matter, you tell us you don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was coming from the Bosnian Croats. The people who were crossing the river on that particular day said they'd only left them a matter of minutes before. So, no, it was clear, I felt, that it was coming from the Bosnian Croat side. Perhaps -- I don't know if I did say this by also saw people crossing in daylight in other front line positions near Bulevar. Again, old -- there was an elderly -- they're also in the film, an elderly couple and another old lady who were just pushed over in daylight and, again, there were a few shots fired over their heads as they -- as they left. And you'll see that in -- the pictures of that in the film.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, the question that I put to you previously was you had been told by women and others that they -- they understood the men were at the Heliodrom. Did the BBC, did your team ever seek to visit and film at the Heliodrom during the time when you were there?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes. In the -- the period when my colleague Eamonn Matthews was making the arrangements for the film we -- he visited the Bosnian Croat authorities in West Mostar and requested their cooperation with our project. Our plan initially was to film on both sides of the lines, age as part of that we asked to go to various places that were in the news, and my understanding was the Heliodrom was one of the places he asked for. The -- however, we did not get the cooperation we were hoping for from that side, so we -- we went into the east side, which is where the film is concentrated.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges, by the way, when you were in East Mostar did you encounter mostly Muslims there or were there also Serbs and Croats there in East Mostar at the time?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Mainly Muslims but quite a few people who were in mixed marriages or who were the products, the children of mixed marriages. The people who come in from the villages around I would say were almost 100 per cent Muslims, but the people who had been living in the city were quite often people who had sections with other different communities. You know, this was quite a common thing in Bosnian cities, that were people who came from mixed ethnic backgrounds. I mean, I remember, for example, there was a doctor at the hospital who didn't want us to film him because his wife and children were on the other side. He had actually been -- on the day that the barricades finally went up, he'd been on the east side of the city and was trapped there. And he wasn't able to get out and he was -- I think he was a Muslim and his wife was a Croat. So as I say there were -- there were numbers of mixed marriages, though, you know it was certainly mainly Muslims there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Can you tell us a bit more about the shelling and sniping as you observed and experienced it?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Sniping was a real danger. There were a number of different places on the east side of Mostar where it was known that there were -- there were dangerous sniper spots. People knew that because people had been killed there by snipers. There was one between -- on Tito Street between the military HQ and the war hospital. Sometimes people just dashed across about a -- I suppose a 25-meter stretch of road. It was a T-junction, and the top of the T was Tito Street, and then there was another road that faced town to the west side of Mostar. So there was a clear shot down that way and a number of people were killed there. There was a way round the back of it which you went through a couple of apartment buildings and a hairdresser shop and you got through to the hospital. Also, on the other side of the city there was another spot, too, where there was a notorious sniper spot. So sniping was a real danger, and shelling also was something which could basically happen at any time of the day or night. Sometimes it would be quite quiet for a while, and the pattern would often be, if it was quiet then people would start coming out trying to get some water. Kids were -- you know, you can't keep kids inside the whole time so they would want to come out and play, even if it was just in the doorway of the shelter or cellar. But shelling could come in at -- really at any time. So that was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: The microphone is working. So I would -- I apologise that I interrupt you, Mr. Scott, and interrupted our witness. Mr. Bowen, you have mentioned sniping now when you talked about your experience in East Mostar and also in your written statement there are several mentioning of sniper activities. My question is if you have observed or if you have been aware of any sniping activities from East Mostar to the west. That means that if the Bosnian Muslim forces did use the same sniper activities as a way of fighting, or it was mainly concentrated on sniping activities from the west side of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't see it happening but I assumed it would have been happening. I assumed that that was a tactic that they'd use. The Bosnian army -- the Bosnian authorities used the -- the Bosnian army used that tactic in Sarajevo. Sniping went both ways across the front line in Sarajevo, and I had no reason to doubt that sniping went both ways across the front lines in Mostar as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bowen, you were present there, and according to what you're saying, you -- you witnessed a shooting, the looting, and as a professional who has travelled the world and the hottest spots in this world, what was your personal impression as a witness to these events? These shots, were they organised? Was it organised fire or was it left to the discretion of the soldiers who were on the ground and who would just fire to destruct themselves? In other words, were those shots a result of a military strategy of a military organisation, or was it a result of individual behaviour of soldiers who were well or not so well organised? What can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say that they were probably quite well-organised. I'd seen the HVO working elsewhere, and they always seemed to me to be well-organised. They had good equipment, good uniforms. On the northern end of that enclave, for example, they had set up search lights.
