So if you drove down the road, and we did this a couple of times, and we were caught in the searchlights and fired upon. They set up the searchlights to catch vehicles and people moving at night. So that shows to me some organisation. They had quite heavy weapons, heavy mortars and tanks. That shows some kind of organisation. What -- it wasn't, you know, constant bang, bang, bang the whole time. Sometimes there'd be a very noisy hour or two hours and then it would be quiet for maybe an hour or two hours, half a day. But generally speaking you'd hear small-arms fire going on quite a bit. As for the sniping activity, you know, it takes only one man to be a sniper but, you know, he has to be quite well-organised in terms of his own skills and the equipment, you know, using a specialist sniper rifle. So I would say it was my assumption -- and also I would say it was pretty organised because also it kept going for quite some time. I'm talking of periods of weeks and months. The other main weapon used to target East Mostar was the big anti-aircraft weapon that was set up on Hum, on the hill that overlooked it, and this was a weapon that terrified everybody on the east side because it was a large-calibre weapon which could cause quite a bit of damage, but also it was really noisy. So when they fired it, the sound of it boomed right round East Mostar, which wasn't a large area. I went, for example, once, to a funeral of a child who had been killed, as it were, by shrapnel wounds and the funeral was held after dark and the child was buried in the cemetery after dark because the cemetery itself was in full view of Hum and the anti-aircraft weapon, and they were very worried that they might be targeted by it while they were there. I mean, to answer your question in a sentence, I'd say to me it seemed organised because I knew that the people behind it were the HVO, who were an organised fighting unit, and it kept on going for quite a period. So therefore it needed a lot of logistic support and soldiers who stuck to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm looking at the time. We have to make a 20-minute break. We will resume at 10 past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to ask a few more questions but also move -- try to move fairly quickly to get to the video. But before we leave the topic of sniping at least for now, were there some locations in East Mostar where in fact there were signs posted warning about sniping?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes, there were, "pazi snajper." And there were signs, and there were also some places where screens had been erected, metal screens to allow people to move with a little bit more safety. But it was always -- I mean, I've done it -- you know, there were some places which you had to cross to get from A to B and that was a place where people would run, and that was -- you know, that was -- in those places it was a common sight. And that was -- I'm talking now of everything that was happening east of the -- of the river Neretva. Obviously things were more intense on the west side, that strip of territory that the Bosnian army held on the west side of the Neretva because that's where most of the actual fighting was going on and where the front lines were. That was -- that was more dangerous again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. On that very point, sir, in terms of the front line being on the west side of the Neretva River, can you tell us what observations you made about the -- the shelling and any patterns of shelling that you encountered at the location of the impacts of shelling?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: There wasn't really a pattern to it, to be quite honest. You had to assume that shelling could come almost anywhere at any particular time. I've -- I was certainly, while I was there, close to the impacts of shells. For example, that were not close to any military position that I could see. You know, I'm sure that if military positions were set up they would try to shell them, too, but they were -- it seemed to me that shells would come in a -- frankly a pretty indiscriminate way into the east side of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Before we leave that topic, could you tell us during the times you were in Mostar, did you see any Bosnian army military positions near the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: No, I didn't see any near the hospital. That's not to say -- you know, I can't say that there weren't any but I didn't see any.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Did you talk during your time in Mostar to any Bosnian army soldiers at the front line about the use of Muslim prisoners?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes. I made a number of visits to front-line positions in Santici and Bulevar, and I also met front-line soldiers who had withdrawn from those positions and were having a bit of time away from the front lines, and with those I was able to have some quite long conversations. And I heard from a number of different sources about the use of Bosnian army prisoners as human shields, effectively, in front of advances. I heard a number of stories, and I think one of them is featured in the film, about how soldiers were -- sorry, prisoners were pushed out to cover an advance behind them by the Bosnian Croat forces, and in fact some of the soldiers I spoke to spoke about how they were forced to throw grenades and to open fire at their own people when they were confronted with this. I also heard from them as well about the use of prisoners to do various forced labour jobs on the front lines, digging trenches, filling sandbags, that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you also hear during your time there about any Croat prisoners who were held on the Muslim side or in East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes. I first saw Croat prisoners there on my first trip in August and it was in the barracks, on the grounds of the northern barracks in Mostar where -- in fact, we were just going along the road and I saw there was a crowd of people and I went to investigate with the camera crew, and there were a group of -- of prisoners who were exhuming bodies, bodies of -- Croat bodies. So there were Croat prisoners digging up Croat bodies, and the idea was that they would use this in some kind of an exchange of bodies. Then later -- so therefore I knew that there were Croat prisoners in East Mostar. When I returned there to film the documentary, as I already knew that there were prisoners there we put in a request to see them, and we were able to -- to see them in a -- they were locked at that particular time in a -- in a -- I can't remember if -- if it was a cellar or a -- or a ground floor room. Anyway, it was a windowless room or a window that was shuttered, lit by artificial light, and they were not allowed to speak to us. I did try to talk to them even though I'd been asked not to, and they were -- they didn't reply. I mean, they were -- just sort of stared ahead of them. They'd obviously been told, I suppose, not to engage us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us in that regard, by the way, when your travelling and filming about Mostar on both visits were any restrictions put on your movement or what you could film by the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: No. Well, the restrictions were -- well, in any war zone the main restriction is danger, where you can go, how you can try -- the big challenge for a journalist is to try to operate in a place like that without becoming a casualty yourself. So we asked for and got guides to take us to front-line positions, and obviously we went to the front-line positions with their consent, because if you're a stranger approaching a front-line position without consent then you're going to be -- you can be -- you can end up getting shot. So you need to have a guide, also to know where to go and the safe way to get there and the relative -- I mean, there was nothing safe but the least dangerous option in terms of trying to get there. You know, for example, we crossed one of the bridges to get to Santici before dawn, very, very early, because we were told that there were Bosnian Croat positions very close by and so we had to -- you know, it have very nerve-wracking, it was pitch black but we had to trip across this bridge to get to those positions so we needed help for those kinds of things but I certainly -- at no point did they say, "You can't do that. You must do this."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: It wasn't like Iraq, where I'd worked quite a bit, where that kind of thing would happen in Iraq. But nothing like that happened in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you say "nothing like that," you mean in terms of having --

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Having a minder or guide who would be, you know, like -- who would actually say, "No, you can't do that." "Yes, you can do this." "Point your camera that way." "Don't point your camera in the other way." That sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You did not have that when you were in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is it correct, sir, that you left East Mostar then in early October, 1993, and returned to London?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes. We returned to -- for the post-production phase of making the documentary. You know, the putting together part of it, the editing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is it correct, sir, that the documentary was then first aired on the BBC in November 1993?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time we would then ask to play the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before that, I have a question that I would like to ask you. You are the first witness who is well suited to answer such a question. According to what you have just told us, you were there around the 15th of August, and then in September you came back. You said that there was a front line. In your assessment, in your view, while you were in East Mostar among those who belonged to the BiH army who were on the Muslim side, in your view could the HVO have taken the front line easily if they had put up an organised attack and could they have occupied East Mostar? Would that have been possible? Or would this have been impossible in military terms, which would explain the permanence -- permanent status of this front line? You're not a military professional, but you are somebody who was there and who have -- had 23 years of experience with front lines. In your view, if the HVO had wanted to do so would they have been able to occupy the entire east side of Mostar by an organised assault action?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was my view that the Bosnian army there were very well organised, as a matter of fact, that they were -- they were highly mobilised. They had got all the men of military age in uniform and fighting. They seemed to be pretty unified in what they were doing. In Sarajevo, for example, you couldn't say that. Different units were -- there was a lot of internal tension in Sarajevo, and I didn't get that in Mostar. I think that they were doing a pretty effective job defending their positions, and their positions were quite -- quite good ones. They were quite secure. I have no idea if the HVO could have brought up more forces and mounted some kind of assault, and I don't know if that's what they wanted to do, but certainly it seemed to me that the Bosnian army forces there were doing a pretty effective job in defending their territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just to clarify this. You have just told us that the HVO was on Hum hill. You have also told us that there were tanks, and you have spoken about shooting and sniper fire. What about this shooting on the east side? Despite the shooting and despite the organisation of the BH army, were they forced to retreat because of the terrain? And there was constant shelling, and would one say this constant shelling was the cause why this military situation could not have been resolved sooner, in a more efficient way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You know, I was not privy to the internal politics of either side. There's a story I think we tell in the film about -- I interviewed a man called General Pasalic, Arif Pasalic, and he said -- he claimed that they had gone a long way to capturing the gun on Hum in an assault sometime before we arrived there and that they'd been asked to -- they'd been ordered to pull back by the -- the BiH military command in Sarajevo because there was -- they wanted to show that they were prepared to respect a cease-fire or something like that. There was a wider political reason for it, in other words. It seemed to me that -- at the time that the HVO looked pretty serious about wanting to take over the whole of Mostar as their capital, and there was at times quite intense exchanges between the -- the two sides. You know, we'd see a pretty steady stream of wounded coming into the hospital, for example. And while I was at the front lines on various -- various visits there was -- you know, there was exchanges of fire. You know, not constant, not all-out intense, intense, intense. You know, for example, a couple of years after that I was in Grozny when the Russians first attacked it, and that was much, much more intent. But by the standards of the Bosnian war it was pretty intense -- very intense in Mostar. And as to your question about whether the HVO could have moved in and taken those positions, the thing about warfare in towns, urban [Realtime transcript read in error, "open"] warfare is very difficult. Again using my experience of Grozny as a yardstick, in Grozny the Russians moved in very heavily with air support, very heavy weaponry. They smashed a concrete and steel city down in weeks yet they couldn't defeat the Chechen fighters. And on a smaller scale I suspect that the HVO, had they mapped to break through would have had problems. The leans, for example, the streets were too narrow in the BiH enclave on the west side of the river Neretva. The streets were too narrow to use in the main to use tanks in. Even if they had tanks they couldn't have used them effectively. So it would have been down to man against man, and that's a -- a lot then is to do with the motivation of different forces and it struck me that the -- the Bosnian forces, the BiH forces in East Mostar were very highly motivated. They really thought that if they didn't fight they'd die. They thought they had nowhere to go and no way out and it was a fight to the death. I heard that from so many different people there that I had to believe it. Quite a few of them told stories of, you know, other male relations that were imprisoned by the Bosnian Croats. They told stories of members of their family who were killed already. They were angry about what was happening to the civilians. They struck me as being very strongly motivated and, as a result, effective fighters.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I raise a point on transcript because it could give rise to misunderstanding. At page 54, line 17, it says "open warfare." I heard urban warfare.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said urban.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's easily misheard. The witness confirms he said "urban." It's easily misheard, so may I observe that on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And my last question before the video: You've told us that you had an interview with General Arif Pasalic. We're certainly going to see that. However, in the conversation with either him or other persons, did -- did he tell you that the solution could not be a military one but that it could only be a political solution? Did you hear anything of such a political solution to the conflict that was going on in Mostar? Did anybody in your interviews, in your talks mention a political solution that was being sought for the situation in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, not particularly. In fact, I asked a lot of them whether what they wanted was a Muslim state, and they all denied it, actually. They didn't say they wanted a Muslim state. I -- to be honest with you, Your Honour, I don't -- I don't recall without my notebook I can't recall the precise details of the conversation you had with -- with Pasalic on the political future. I think -- in a lot of people I spoke to there, perhaps he was one of them as well, there was a feeling that ultimately it would come down to politics, but, you know, essentially talking to people there, they were in a very immediate, day-to-day fight, and their horizons were not that high. You know, they were trying to get through the next day very often.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Mr. Scott, the video please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] This morning we were trying to repair our wall."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, if I could just ask you a couple of questions about what we just saw, just some points of clarification. In an early part of the documentary you said something to the effect -- I think I wrote it down correctly, that the HVO was aided and abetted by the Croatian government. Can you tell the Judges what you based that on, what information you had or knowledge that you gained at that time that you based that on?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I based that on what I already knew about Mostar about the links between Herceg-Bosna and Zagreb. I got that information partly from conversations with people in Zagreb, from the meeting I talked about with -- with Mr. Kordic in Busovaca. While I was there as well, they pointed out to me that they -- they showed me ID papers of Croatian regulars and people from Zagreb who they had taken these papers they said from prisoner and from bodies. And in addition, at that particular in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the whole projects of Greater Croatia and for that matter Greater Serbia is something that people spoke about on a regular basis and people also spoke about it in Zagreb and in -- for the Serbian project in Belgrade as well. It was the kind of thing that was in contemporary discourse. It didn't seem to be a secret. It was -- it seemed to be part of the -- part of the weather, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I comment. Mr. Scott didn't actually quite write it down correctly. What it says -- I'm not arguing about it but it does actually say, "Since May Bosnian Croats aided and abetted by the Croatian government ..." Just for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think that's a very, very close statement but, of course, I think the video will speak for itself but I think the point is made.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, there was the footage -- there was a -- night-time footage we saw of a group of Muslims coming across a bridge. Do you happen to recall -- were you able to remember the date of that particular event?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: It was towards the end of September. I did have the date and I think I put it in my witness statement because I went back to the cassette to get the date from. Was it the 29th of September? From memory I can't quite remember but I know the date I put it in my witness statement was based -- as I say, I'd gone back to the original tape. We always put the dates that the tapes were shot, on the rushes tapes, so I would go with the date that was in my witness statement which, I'm sorry, at the moment I can't recall precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just let me look for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, if necessary, I can show the witness his statement. I think everyone in the courtroom has it. I might just read that part of the statement to him since he's already referred to it as being in his statement, but I'll proceed in however the Chamber would like me to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we accept that in the statement it does indicate the night of the 29th September, 1993. That's what's in the statement. We can just proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karnavas. If I can just look at my notes for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The group that you saw coming across that night, the 29th of September, 1993, can you tell us was that the largest single group you saw coming across from West Mostar during the time that you were there?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes, it was the largest group I saw. And I'd been disappointed a couple of nights earlier because they'd said, "Oh," you know, "You'd already gone to bed but a whole group of people came across the river." So we said to them, "Look, if it happens again, come and get us." So that's what they did, and that was the biggest single group that I saw. I was interested, by the way, in my -- to clarify something. In the script there I said they were trying to kill them and here in the testimony I said it seemed like harassing fire. I think that's just what memory does. You know, 14 years ago when I was there I thought that their intentions were to kill. So maybe that was more accurate than what I said before we saw the film.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, I think based on the questions the Judges have asked and other questions and comments you've made, that really concludes the questions I have for you. I want to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and giving your evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to give the floor to the Defence teams. As regards the time that Mr. Stewart has asked for, there has been a misunderstanding. In a decision that we rendered, the word was about the supplementary time and we have stated that the Defence would have one and a half hours. Unless they agree differently, they will split the time among themselves. So that means that Mr. Petkovic's Defence can have up to one hour and a half. We are, unfortunately, obliged to divide the time in six. Who is going to start? If we divide the time in six, that means 15 minutes for every Defence team. Maybe some Defence teams will not have any questions to ask. Who is going to start, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour, but that still leaves me rather unclear. Since I don't know what's happening with the other Defence teams, I shall stop at the end of 15 minutes, shan't I? Is Your Honour saying if there's time left at the end I can have that as well later?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe a solution suggested by my colleague is to have a break of 20 minutes during which time the Defence teams will talk. And I have already told you that you had the time to prepare for the week, and that with regard to this witness you should have talked and you should have agreed who would cross-examine this journalist from the BBC which would have avoided everybody asking the same questions about the same topic. We are going to make a 20-minute break, and maybe amongst yourselves you're going to be able to agree on who is going to use most of the time or maybe all the time, because this is how you should work. Or maybe you want to use up your 15 minutes, each of you. Within the 15 minutes, of course, you can't ask that many questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just ask before Your Honour leaves, I say nothing at the moment about Your Honour's observations just then, though I do please reserve the position. Can we just ask whether the Prosecution just had an hour and a half. We assume it includes the documentary. It's just we've been in court rather a long time, and I know that the calculations get complicated, but did the Prosecution have one and a half hours or did they have something different in the end?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One hour and 34 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I asked the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have gotten that from the registry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm not going to make a major issue of four minutes and how it's split amongst six people, although I suppose I reserve the right to have another 40 seconds [Realtime transcript read in error, "minutes"] if I'm pushed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stewart, you have the floor since you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you. Sorry. I anticipated, Your Honour, being on my feet. I beg your pardon or I hadn't bothered to sit down. Your Honour, I think there's a correction on the transcript. I talked about 40 seconds rather than 40 minutes immediately before the break. There is a difference. Your Honour, on the point that I said I would simply reserve my position before the break, Your Honour, it is -- we understand what Your Honour is proposing, but it's actually unreal to expect six Defence teams to get together and have the sort of discussion that Your Honour has in mind. In the last break we spent the time with our client, which has to be rather a serious priority, but if Your Honour just please thinks or Your Honours think of the exercise of six Defence teams getting together to discuss what questions they will ask in cross-examination, what topics they will cover, it really is just unreal. We can't do that. We end up with a certain amount of -- or sometimes it's horse trading. Parties consider whether it's in their own client's interest to give their time to somebody else. But we're left -- it has to be some sort of indulgence. We have no right to have any more time, so at the moment I'm simply left under the allocation of 15 minutes and I return to my original submission that 15 minutes just isn't long enough for anybody to conduct a cross-examination of a serious witness, and the result is it's a bit like six people have got to be somewhere 12 miles away, you can't just say, well, each of them go two miles because you don't get there, Your Honour. It's just -- it's just completely useless, these small chunks. Well, I say "completely useless"; people may judge my cross-examination in that way. But these small chunks of time for serious cross-examination just will not work, Your Honour, and I know it all happened before I came here but I'm not aware from my discussions with Mrs. Alaburic, my lead counsel, that we have signed up to this arrangement. We have consistently protested when necessary and asked for more time when necessary and we do repeat our position on that, Your Honour, that it's deeply unsatisfactory. I don't know whether anybody else wants to say anything before I now embark on such cross-examination as I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I could just make one brief --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please, Mr. Karnavas, before you take the floor. I listened carefully to what Mr. Stewart was saying, and while he was speaking I was looking at the six documents of the Petkovic Defence and I was wondering and thinking that during the time he was speaking I would have had time to present the six documents to the witness. So there we have it. Now, Mr. Karnavas, if you wish to waste more time, then go ahead, but it would be better to ask useful questions of the journalist that we have here rather than wasting time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I agree, Mr. President. I do wish to put on the record that the gentleman spoke about a variety of issues concerning the indictment such as the joint criminal enterprise, wide and systematic attacks in a national armed conflict, and so on and so forth. And might I also appointment out just briefly that we spent 45 minutes watching a video that we all watched before coming here and we could have watched at some other point in time when we had some free time and this would have allotted us more time for cross-examination. I certainly don't see this as good management time on behalf of the Prosecution, and I think that we are the victims of not having sufficient time now to cross-examine the gentleman.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say that Petkovic Defence like every Defence in this case is entitled both to cross-examine and make appropriate submissions on procedural matters, and I have exercised my right and done my duty to my client in making that submission and, Your Honour, with respect, we will not be deterred by the suggestion that we should have done something else while we were "wasting time." We're not wasting time, Your Honour, by making cogent submissions, even if they are rejected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, for the record I would like to state that I fully agree with what my colleagues have said. I don't wish to take up more time. I fully endorse what they said, and I'd just like to add that we consider that every Defence team is a separate Defence team in this trial, and every accused has the right to their time and has the right to challenge any witness's testimony if he feels that he needs to do so. So this distribution of time amongst ourselves, which we do do whenever possible, when we manage to reach an agreement, can not be interpreted in any other way but bartering time amongst ourselves. All of us merit raising questions on any salient point, and, as my colleagues Mr. Stewart and Mr. Karnavas said, there are a few vital subjects which enter into the critical passages in the indictment. Given 15 minutes' time or one and a half hours for all of us, we just cannot do the job properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would also like to put on the record that I agree with what Mr. Stewart has said. I needn't take up any more time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, one minute, one minute. They've taken I think about 15 minutes, so let me have one minute. Your Honour, this comment by Mr. Karnavas is completely inappropriate. Of course we put on our evidence. We used exactly -- almost exactly the time the Chamber gave us. We'd asked for two hours. The Chamber cut us to an hour and a half. We put on the evidence. We don't put on the evidence publicly, we get complaints that the evidence hasn't been put on publicly. If we do -- you know, it's the old whatever you do it's wrong. We object to that. We have to put on our case. The Prosecution manages to put on its case, also under protest, I might add. The Chamber knows our position on the time we've been allowed but we try to go forward the best we can. And now once again, once again we spent another 20 minutes on these matters whatever they may be, but we don't have to do this every day. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber has deliberated, and we have decided that you should start off within the 15 minutes that you have and if there are any important questions that remain we can always be flexible. But we must weigh up the relevance of the questions because if you're going to speak about everything and nothing, then that won't be that important. So start off and we'll see whether you realistically need more time to broach certain issues that are necessary. I should like to remind you without making any reference, precise references to -- the rulings of the Appeals Chamber is that the cross-examination is not an absolute right, and that cross-examination as a process must follow certain rules and regulations and restrictions and that it must be linked to the questions raised by the Prosecution and the Judges and so on and so forth. So start off and we'll see whether there are any questions that you did not have time to raise, and then we'll see whether to grant you additional time or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, I'm sure you found that edifying. Good afternoon. Mr. Bowen, you've probably gathered that Ms. Alaburic next to me and I represent Mr. Petkovic who was on his feet earlier. Mr. Bowen, in -- in the documentary right towards the end of your evidence you had asked Mr. Humo, you said, "What if your military efforts are undercut by President Izetbegovic signing a piece of paper that says we have a cease-fire just where we are now and we stop fighting? Would you accept that?" Could I just be clear. Does that bit of the documentary come from recordings made on your second visit in September 1993?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: All the interviews with Humo were recorded in that second visit, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: At that time do you recall or do you know that in fact there had already been by the time you returned to Mostar a piece of paper signed by President Izetbegovic and by President Tudjman, a joint declaration for a cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: This is your document here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It is one of the documents there; that's absolutely right. It's document P 05051. It's the first document in your bundle.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yeah, I had a quick look at it. I was aware that -- one of the things that I found through four years of covering all the various wars in -- in Bosnia -- in the former Yugoslavia between 1991 and 1995 is that there were very often cease-fires and very often they had no effect at all on the ground. I almost lost count of the times where I would be listening to the BBC World Service on my shortwave radio telling me that a cease-fire had been signed when we were taking shelter from shelling somewhere, in a place where a cease-fire was supposedly holding. So as a reporter in the area, I never attached a great degree of credence to statements made in -- you know, far from the fighting in places like Geneva. I always went more by what I saw myself on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But you were aware, then, were you, when you had this exchange with Mr. Humo that there had already been such a piece of paper just a week or so previously?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I can't remember in detail if I was aware of this particular thing, but I can say that I imagine my reaction would have within, "We've heard about cease-fires lots of times; let's see if it actually holds." My feeling, my sort of journalistic analysis of the policy of cease-fires is very often they came as a result of outside pressure and didn't actually reflect a will to have a cease-fire among the protagonists in the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were you aware that there had been in August a -- an agreement for a cease-fire but then a revival of really quite serious plans on the part of the Bosnia-Herzegovina army for offensive action against the HVO?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of any of their plans, and I found it interesting looking at some of these documents because at the time, obviously things like public joint declarations we would have had access to but secret military orders, no, I mean, we had no idea about. Before I went to Mostar I went to the office of Rasim Delic in Sarajevo, for example, and we got no information about those kinds of things. So, no, I was not aware of their offensive plans.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The action that you describe in the documentary on Mount Hum, the -- the -- well, successful action as far as the army were concerned but then rather called to a halt by directions, orders from Sarajevo, that was part of -- of an action or was known as Neretva 93. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I haven't heard that code word ever, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And -- and do you recall, is this correct, that by certainly a few days before you arrived there had been -- whatever peace discussions and declarations there'd been, there had been a concerted continuation of offensive activities by the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean, they told me that they'd had this -- this assault. A war was going on there. You know, I -- in no sense in my reporting there did I suggest that one side was attacking the other side wasn't. You know, it was a war. It was a two-way street. They fought each other. I personally would very much have liked to have been able to cover the Bosnian Croat side in the detail I was able to cover the BiH government side, but we didn't -- couldn't get access so I wasn't able to do it. You know, I wasn't there to -- I mean, essentially I was there to report what was happening at a given time. That's how I saw my particular job.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were you aware of any -- an order made subsequently by Mr. Delic on the 30th of September? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: 30th September. No. No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What I have in mind, Mr. Bowen -- it's all right Mr. Praljak is going to pick up that point.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: All right, fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So I'll leave that for the moment then. At page --

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Is that the other document that's here?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It -- don't worry about it, Mr. Bowen; that's fine. Mr. Praljak is going to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: At page 24 of the transcript of the documentary you talked about the -- the order coming from Sarajevo telling them to retreat, the government wanted to accepted a positive signal and you mentioned that in your evidence. Then you go on to a question of supply of ammunition. All right, it may not have been the conventional ideal method of bringing in ammunition but it was a fact, wasn't it, that pretty substantial amounts of ammunition were being brought into -- into Mostar by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I guess it depends how you deep fine substantial. It was certainly steady, as far as I could see. And on the caravan of horses that I travelled with most of the -- you know, it wasn't -- it was mainly mortar bombs, which suggested that you know they had the mortars to fire them out of. No, they had the tools, I think, to do their job, to a degree, anyway. Certainly when it came to fairly light infantry weapons. They didn't have quite so much in terms of heavier weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But they were clearly able to sustain this concerted offensive action, weren't they, and were frustrated when orders from elsewhere stepped in?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yeah, they were -- as I said, they were highly motivated and they were fighting the war in a very efficient way. One the characteristics of the first year or so of the war from the BiH government side is, frankly, they were often a bit chaotic. What impressed me about the BiH forces in East Mostar was that they were well organised. They got their act together and they were fighting efficiently and effectively.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You refer in the -- in the documentary to the independent-minded Mostar commanders. You -- you've indicated their dissatisfaction about orders from Sarajevo, that -- just in case, "independent-minded Mostar commanders are buying weapons from the Serbs as well." Independent-minded sounds like a little bit of a euphemism there. Was it actually that they were inclined to go against what they were being ordered from above?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: No, that wasn't the impression I had. You know, for example, Pasalic, I had a few conversations with him and he said they weren't -- they followed the orders but they weren't happy with them. They felt -- they felt essentially that the authorities of Sarajevo were not prosecuting the war with the determination that they were doing and that if they only did that in Sarajevo then they'd get much further in the war themselves. They basically wanted the people in Sarajevo to fight a bit harder.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I want to ask you a bit about the events on the 29th of November. You've put a date on it --

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Of September, I beg your pardon. Thank you for the correction. 29th of September. In your statement, and I'm talking about the most reaccept statement you've given -- I don't know whether you have a copy in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You don't, I wonder.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: At least I don't think -- maybe I do. Wait a minute, there are some documents it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'll read it and then if we run into any difficulty or anybody tells me I'm reading it wrong we'll --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please make a pause between questions and answers for the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Okay. You said that during -- it's on page 4 of the statement for everybody's reference, and it's the second full paragraph. "During both of my trips to East Mostar in August and September 1993 there was always at the least a constant trickle of Muslims coming into East Mostar from the west side or from other areas in the region. On some days or nights the number of Muslims coming into East Mostar increased dramatically. These people had been expelled from their homes and villages by the Bosnian Croat forces. The 'Unfinished Business' documentary contains footage taken during the night of 29th September, 1993, of a large number of Muslims being expelled into East Mostar." You'll see I'm slowing down, Mr. Bowen. "On this night approximately 200 people were expelled into East Mostar." The documentary says 500. Your statement says 200. What -- can you explain that discrepancy?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I think it's probably again the effects of memory. I wrote the script for the documentary with the notebooks I had there and the notes I'd taken. And with it very fresh in my mind I wrote the script probably three weeks, maximum, after the event, and that statement was several years after the event. More than several years. I think it was --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, it certainly was, Mr. Bowen.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: It was probably seven or eight years after the event. So that's just, I think, a slip of memory. I personally would go with the number closer to the time as the more -- the more accurate one, and I think when I made the statement I probably didn't recall I'd said 500 in the film because I hadn't seen the film at that point in some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Okay. So 500. And then you go on in the statement - I want to make sure I'm sticking with the statement at the moment - that, "With the Bosnian Croat forces shooting at them or over their heads as they crossed a small foot bridge over the river Neretva." Now, just to make it clear what I'm saying, there is no reference I could find in the documentary transcript of shooting over their heads. So this seems to be, if you like, this is an improvement of your memory because this ties in with what you've told the Court this morning or this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes. Shooting over their heads or shooting at them. Well, the next day as we saw in the film there was one a body lying in no man's land who somebody had killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You're talking about the woman?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, that was the route that they'd taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was that the one you said was skilled by a sniper? Was that --

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, the next morning they said -- they came to us the next morning and said, "By the way, those people who came over, the route that they took, we can see the route that they took and there's a new body lying there." Because, you know, they kept the places under observation. They could tell, so we went then to that front line position.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, you said the -- you said earlier today in your evidence-in-chief that nobody was hit. You didn't suggest that that woman -- she was put in the documentary as being killed by a sniper. You didn't suggest that she was somebody -- you said in terms that nobody was hit.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: No, I meant when they were crossing the river.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Right. So nobody was hit when they were crossing the river. By the way, the position was this, wasn't it, that the -- of course there were Muslims on the east side of the river and then but the Muslim front line was on the other side of the Neretva wasn't it? So you --

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yeah, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So you then --

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: You're familiar with the map as I am. You will see that in some places it was quite wide and some places it wasn't so wide.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So on that night 500, and you've gone for 500 this morning, so 500 near enough cross over, and --

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Or -- if I can just interrupt. All those numbers that journalists give in these things are an estimate based on what they saw at the time. It's not particularly scientific. You know, what you do is you see the room they've pitched up in and you try and work out roughly how many there were. I certainly didn't count them individually.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, I'm not going to suggest anything different.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I accept that. It's just that as between 200 and 500, you --

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- you've gone with the 500, so I said near enough -- for working purposes, several hundred people?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Not one of them -- according to you, not one of them was actually hit. It would be fair to say, wouldn't it, Mr. Bowen, that if one or more of them had been hit and had clearly hit, it's a racing certainty that you would have included that in the documentary, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: No. I mean -- as I said in my earlier testimony, the -- there were a lot of -- of bullets flying around as they crossed the river, and while I absolutely agree that there were BiH forces on both sides of the river, you know the -- the range of a Kalashnikov is, you know, is 600 metres more than that I think in the hands of a good soldier, and that's assuming they were using Kalashnikovs and not weapons with -- which fired with a greater range than that. So I had no reason to suppose that they were firing on their own people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, I'm sorry, what I'm putting to you is this that what you were describing this morning was, was actually essentially correct and that they were not actually trying to kill people, whereas in the documentary you said unequivocally that they were trying to kill women and children and that's not what you've said this morning?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: You know, as I say, that might be the dilution effect of memory because, now that we're talking about it, you know, I remember the feeling of being there and hearing the bullets whistling around my head. As I said -- and you can hear it on the soundtrack, incoming bullets coming near your head displace air and it makes a very specific noise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But isn't the position this --

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I certainly felt that evening -- I was very conscious, for example, that because we'd gone out there in a hurry I wasn't wearing my flak jacket. I didn't have my helmet. I could hear the bullets going around me and -- so I guess I drew the conclusion that they were out to kill. Maybe they just didn't hit anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But maybe --

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: And maybe -- let me just finish. Maybe after this many years I'm giving the HVO forces more credit than they deserve - I don't know - in terms of whether they were able to hit the people they -- they were firing at.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, I apologise. I'm caught between the courtesies of not interrupting the witness and the pressure of time.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I'll try and keep it short.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You're doing very well, thank you. Mr. Bowen, it's -- what I'm putting to you is that what you said this morning makes common sense, that given the -- where they were, the fact that nobody was actually -- let's leave aside that poor woman for the moment, but the fact that nobody was killed was at the time sufficiently strong indication that they had not intended to kill anybody for it not to have been correct to have said in unqualified terms in the documentary that that's what they were trying to do. I am putting that to you fairly and squarely, Mr. Bowen.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: And I would say that it's probably a mistake to overlook the woman whose body that we saw, who was killed in the course of that exodus.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, you're the one that overlooked it, Mr. Bowen, earlier in your evidence.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes, well, I did. I -- to be honest with you, I'd probably forgotten that we had that picture. I hadn't seen this -- this film for quite some time and, since it was there, and I will always think that these things, it's better to go with what you said at the time rather than what you say 14 years later.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to move on from that, Mr. Bowen.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm looking at the clock. I do submit that that was a reasonable area to explore and that inevitably a detailed area like that takes quite a few minutes. So I may I continue with my next topic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your next topic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It almost is as quick to put it as to describe it, Your Honour, but I'm going into the question of the references in the documentary to the Croats and various other terms used for the Croats. May I -- Your Honour, may I just put it -- it really will be about as quick to put it, leaving aside the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, you refer to Bosnian Croats -- you often refer, and I'm not criticising this at all, you refer to "the Croats" and "their Croat enemies," and so on, "a Croat sniper," and then at page 17 of the -- of the transcript we get a reference to the Croat extremists and that follows a reference to the Croat gangs and you're using the phrase "Croat gangs" to describe people you are reporting as having expelled people from West Mostar, and then you use the phrase -- and you say, "the brutality of the expulsions drives home the message that compromise with Croat extremists is neither possible nor desirable." And, first of all, I'm asking you what you meant by the phrase "the Croat extremists." It's the only time in this transcript that you use such a phrase, apart from the gangs.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: It was strong language -- gangs and extremists, I agree, are strong language. However, I'd done probably several dozen interviews, some quite extensive at only a fraction of which made it on air with people who had been expelled forcibly by groups of young armed men, who treated them brutally, from their homes in the middle of the night you know, women, children, old people with these -- and I can only say gangs of young men coming and kicking them out of their houses. I thought in the circumstances it's a strong word but its a fair one. I also -- by that -- this point in the war in Bosnian, the phrase "ethnic cleansing" was something that was often used. The concept was well-known, and I felt that groups that practised ethnic cleansing were practising an extreme form of political action trying to -- to if you like create -- change the ethnic demographic composition of places by force, and I felt that it's reasonable in the circumstances to describe that as extreme behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So when you refer to the Croat extremists there, you're not referring then to the -- to the -- the regular authorities if you understand what I mean the regular governmental authorities?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I'm referring to anybody who is responsible for the people doing it at such an organised scale. The scale in which it was happening could not reasonably be described as -- as accidental or anything other than coordinated. It was happening with such regularity that it had to be coordinated, so I would say that whoever was giving the orders to the people to drive, as I say, these defenseless civilians out of their homes in the middle of the night at gunpoint beating them and taking away the men and, in the case of the woman who was interviewed who had been told that her two sons had had their throats cut, killing them, according to her, what she was saying, and there were many other stories as well of men being taken off and never being seen again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, may I --

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: The point I'm making --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- hurdle, we have seen all this --

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I just felt that "extremist" was a fair use of the word.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So you say Croat -- compromise with Croat extremists is neither possible nor desirable. Compromise with those in positions of higher authority would have been obviously desirable, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I wasn't -- the impression that I tried to give through that sentence and maybe I didn't make it as sharp as I could have was not, this is my view, but this is the impression taken from this by the mainly Muslim defenders of East Mostar. They felt that there was no point trying to compromise with people who were capable of doing things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you agree that your label of ethnic cleansing there's a sort of template is that a fair word to describe it for each scene you have a you've got six you've got about eight topics and you mark them for each scene -- I call it a template, I don't know, perhaps you've got a jargon name in the business for it.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: On your transcript on each scene, I assume it's yours rather than anybody else's, it says --

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I wrote it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You say "rape" and then "military/paramilitary," the various topics on each page. Do you need a reminder as to what it looks like? I thought you had seen the transcript of your ...

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: The transcript is on my desk here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Just give me --

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Give me a --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- at -- what, page 17 is what I'm looking at here.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You see at the bottom of the page "rape," yes, is marked do you see what I mean?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: 17, it's in French, the one I've got.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, it's probably there --

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Hang on. English. No, sorry, sorry, sorry, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- or something like that.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Wait a second, I've got it here in English, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Oh, that was -- that must have been added by the people here. I mean, that's -- this is not my script. This is a -- this is a transcript which has been prepared by the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's OTP note or something?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: -- by the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I was hopelessly confused by that, and --

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: It's nothing. No, I -- if only we were that organised. Well, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Well, we should withdraw all that then. But so far as ethnic cleansing is concerned, not a label on the piece of paper then, but as your label, do you agree that your term, "ethnic cleansing," would cover a single incident by a small group of the brutal nature that you describe in your documentary at one end of the spectrum to the at the other end of the spectrum, as a matter of definition, would cover an orchestrated campaign and policy at the highest level. So it would cover the whole range wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Well, I mean, you could define it like that, but I think you can only use words that describe whole trends or policies like that if it's a repeated pattern of behaviour. And by that point in the -- you know, if it only happened once, if only one family had ever been evicted by a group of armed men, then I would -- probably wouldn't call it ethnic cleansing but since it was happening so much, and not just in this theatre of war, it was, I feel -- I'm not sure I even used the phrase in the film itself, but ethnic cleansing is a -- is a phrase that people understand and I think the most -- the best definition of it is something which is an overall policy, and, of course, every big policy is made up of lots of individual actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, the time question is greatly helped by fact that the person I would cross-examine, if I had the chance, would be Mr. Scott on that template, as I described it, and since that's not possible, I don't need to pursue that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Just so there's no mistake in the record, the transcripts that are before you is -- are exactly as received from the BBC, and I can understand that it was apparently an indexing system used by the BBC. You will notice in the first page of the English version, video archive and database. I suppose like most news organisation or large people who deal with large amounts of data and information there is an archive and there is a coding -- an indexing system.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Observing, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So this was not added by the OTP; it came from the BBC exactly as here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's extremely helpful, and I have to make no application to cross-examine Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I then go to that? The -- that is -- you -- you were not involved in this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stewart, my colleagues feel that you have used up your time and that we should stop you. What question is it that you would like to ask that would be useful, as far as the Judges are concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because do not forget that the questions that you're asking are ones that should be designed to have a result for the Judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, for the Judges in performance of our duty to Mr. Petkovic. Exactly, Your Honour, the twin -- twin aims. I do know -- by the way, I should say, Your Honour, I do know that Mr. Petkovic himself wishes to put two short questions. But all I wanted to ask the witness -- Your Honour, since the witness appears to have no particular knowledge of this template, I'll - he's shaking his head; he clearly doesn't - I'll drop it there, Your Honour. Sorry, excuse me, Your Honour. Apparently -- good news for Your Honours is Mr. Petkovic does not have questions, Your Honours, so thank you for the -- for the additional time. That is appreciated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I was just about too give Mr. Petkovic the floor. I was ready to do that but if he doesn't have any questions let's move on to the next Defence team. Mr. Karnavas, you're turning to your fellow counsels.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we do not have any questions for this witness and we have given our time to the Praljak Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have also placed our time at the Praljak Defence's disposition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, again. I will indulge in a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll be very focused on what I'm trying to get at and that is the title of your -- ever your documentary is "Unfinished Business," and I think it is quite apropos because, obviously, you never got to the other side, you know, to at least get their side of the story. So from my perspective it is rather unfinished. Would you not say that?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I think it was a finished -- I tell you what, we said "unfinished business" because the war wasn't over. I mean, that was the purpose of the title.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But you never went on the other side?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: The producer went on the other side before we started filming to try to arrange something we did on the BiH side but, as I said earlier, he -- unfortunately the cooperation was not forthcoming.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, so you say. Were you aware that other British journalists were able to go to the other side and get interviews on tape?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Maybe they were, but these things were never consistent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, did you, sir, you personally, did you make any efforts yourself, not your producer but you?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I -- on that particular -- on that particular trip, no, I didn't because my producer had gone there to arrange the work --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm not asking you --

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: -- the meetings and so, therefore, I didn't, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We're going to go step-by-step.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. You're in country for some time. You say back in 1992 you had an opportunity to meet with Mr. Kordic; right?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I did, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, you hear about this story sometime in August 1993 and you decide that you're going to chase that lead.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you here about the Ho Chi Minh trail and so you decide, why not, let's go for it, and that's exactly what you did. Right?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, prior to going there did you consult with any or try to get a hold of any Croats to see whether you could also get their point of view because obviously you're only getting one side of the --

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: You mean on the first trip.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: On the first trip.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: No, I didn't. What I was trying to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm just -- okay --

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- going step-by-step --

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: All right. Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I know you're trying to --

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I'm trying to answer your questions further down the line -- okay. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So you go there. You see that there is a story. You make some -- you do probably file some stories from the first trip. Then when you go back to London, that's when you have this opportunity to go back and do the video; right? Am I correct on that?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, before going back into -- into Mostar, did you yourself, I know you have a producer, but did you yourself do any research? Regarding Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I did some reserve. I didn't do much between the two trips because I'd just been there and I was recovering from the first one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But did you for instance try to figure out who is on the other side, where the political structure lies?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You did?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yeah, sure I got information and I read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, now, from reading that material did you make any efforts, for instance, to contact Mr. Boban to see if he would give you permission to go into West --

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Did I personally, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah. Okay. Now, do you know whether this individual, your producer, actually called him?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Did he ever tell you exactly who he contacted and who said no to him?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: If he did, I don't recall it. I know he spent several days trying to make it happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Where was he during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: He was -- I think he was staying in a hotel in Medjugorje and he was travelling to the west side of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, but according -- surely you would have had notes if he would have told you the names of the individuals he saw? For instance, maybe starting with who was at the HVO in the political leadership or further up the chain, he would have passed those names on to you; right?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: That's not how it works. You know, he's a trusted very experienced colleague so if he says to me, "Look, I went there. I tried for a couple of days. It didn't happen." I didn't cross-examine him as to why it didn't happen; I took his word for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. And did you ever bother to call Mr. Kordic to see whether he could be -- he would be able to assist you in any way?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I -- there were no telephones. I didn't have -- if Mr. Kordic had a satellite telephone number, I certainly didn't have it. There were -- throughout the war there was almost no phone contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, you went to Central Bosnia before; right? That's where you --

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yeah, sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I guess -- again, I don't want to try to pin you down, but before going to Mostar, I mean obviously you had the story in mind when you went back the is second time; right? You're shaking your head?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: No, I'm shaking -- I'm agreeing. I'm nodding. I'm nodding.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, but we need to make a record.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Sure okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm not trying to be obnoxious. You had a story in mind you obviously knew there were two sides to the story; right? You're shaking your head again.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I agree with you. I saw -- I know that there are two sides to a story.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And obviously you probably wanted to get both sides of the story.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yeah, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And all we know today is what you're telling us, and that is that this producer told you that you could not go on the other side to do any filming.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, you also said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. The questions that you're asking, Mr. Karnavas, are ones that I wanted to ask. You're a journalist, sir, a high-level journalist. You work for the BBC, which is well-known all over the world, and you have the chance of being in an area, in a zone where important events are taking place. Now, as far as I know, in August and September UNPROFOR was also there. Now, a journalist of your renown and competent reporting from the area, it would be normal for you to give all sides of the problem. How come you didn't contact UNPROFOR perhaps to -- to say to them, "Is it not possible for me representing the BBC to cross over to the other side to interview Mr. Boban, Mr. X, Y, or Z, so that I can have that view and not only the one on the east bank"? Did that idea come to mind at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not specifically. I was in contact with UNPROFOR at different times, not while I was actually in -- the only contacts I had with UNPROFOR while I was in Mostar itself were with the Spanish soldiers who were there. The thing about working for big news organisation like the BBC is that on the first trip that we did, I wasn't doing a documentary. I was doing daily news reports. We also had coverage from the west side of Mostar. We had a team working in Zagreb who had come regularly to Medjugorje and would go on to the west side of Mostar. We had another team who was with the UNHCR convoy that came in, in late August. So I was part of a wider news operation. We had, for example, a cameraman, a Croatian guy, who lived -- well, we based him in Zagreb. He had a motorcycle, and he spent weeks and the west side of Mostar getting pictures and talking to people. When I was unable to -- so that's when I was doing the news story.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to stop you. We're discovering here, and this wasn't evident up to now, that the BBC had teams deployed in the area, one covering the Mostar west side, the other one the east bank, and others that were attached to humanitarian convoys and so on. Now, between these members of the BBC teams that were divided into different groups, did you have contacts amongst yourselves? You had a satellite telephone, as you told us, and I assume that the others did, too. So did you keep in contact and exchange information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Communications were really difficult, even with a satellite telephone. Satellite telephones at that time were very -- were quite primitive compared to how they work now. They didn't work very well. They used up a great deal of current and power, so we spared the battery a lot of the times. I used them for the bare minimum. Sometimes it was too dangerous to set it up. We were working under -- you know, it was -- there was a lot of pressure there and, frankly, I didn't have time to talk to my colleagues about what they were doing. I thought, They can do what they're doing; I'll do what I'm doing, and it's up to the people in London to coordinate them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Now, the west bank teams, could your colleagues have asked for an interview with Mr. Boban, for example?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sure they did, and I'm -- they weren't constantly in the west side of Mostar through the month of August but I know they visited. I would say that I'm sure that they -- I'm sure that Mr. Boban gave interviews to the BBC during that period. I'm certainly sure that if he didn't give them that they asked for it. It's very typical that we would have almost a constant bid in for an interview with a leader of his importance and stature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, I give you the floor again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. I think you shortened cross-examination quite a bit and I appreciate the questions posed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, it would appear sir from your answers that, had you wanted to go on the other side, at that moment you could have?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: At least that is what I'm reading between the lines.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Can I -- could I answer that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Before you answer that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I would appreciate if I don't get any comments from the peanut gallery because Mr. Scott now is commenting. So go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Then don't mischaracterise the evidence Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, then you can stand up and you can object.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I do object.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What I'm reading between the lines, sir, is you never made one single effort yourself to go on the other side. You didn't go through Zagreb. You didn't call your contacts. You hadn't made any efforts, and I'm putting to you that we've had witness here, other Brits, journalists, maybe not as experienced as you, that at that same period of time were able to go into the west side and meet with the leadership of the Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: There's a difference between going there to do a quick news interview and going there to do a big documentary. I think that if I'd turned up there with a camera crew and stood outside the headquarters and put in -- maybe I would have got an interview. But there's a very big difference between getting one interview and getting the kind of weeks-long access that you need to put together a documentary film. You have to make a distinction between a single, freestanding documentary and the overall news story.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bowen --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- we saw the documentary a moment ago. Technically speaking, the BBC could have made the same document on the other side, along the front line.
