The BBC could have made a documentary with HVO soldiers, for instance, who could have explained why they were fighting, why they were there and so on. The same documentary could have been made the other side, on the west bank. Would you agree with that? Would that have been possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I wouldn't. I mean, that's the point I'm making. We asked for that kind of a facility with the Bosnian Croats in West Mostar, and that request was denied.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: We would very much, I would very much have been like to be able to get to the other side and interview those soldiers. But the point is, when my very experienced colleague, much -- 10 years older than me and a veteran of very many, very serious documentaries went there and tried to make it happen and didn't succeed, I was certainly prepared to take his word for it and not in our limited time go back to ask the same questions again of those same people. You know, it's an -- a division of labour when you're making these films.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just for the record, Your Honour on page 2094 you will have seen and perhaps remembered that we had another witness, Ms. Giles here on -- who apparently was able to make an interview on 28 August, 1993. I point that for the record. It was on the West side and so this was with Mr. Prlic. She was making a documentary at the same point in time. In any event, sir -- in any event, sir, thank you very much for your evidence. Good luck in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The following team, please. Mr. Murphy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Bowen.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: When you introduced yourself to the Court today, you said that you had in the course of your career covered all the big stories. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Most, yeah. I think pretty much between -- when I was a London-based foreign correspondent between 1988 and 1995, I went to every big story.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And you gave one particular example, I think, of what had happened in China after the revolution -- or attempted revolution in the square there, and you said that was a big story?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: It was a big story, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And when you heard from Mr. Kasselman at the press conference, started to learn about Mostar, that was also a big story?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Kessler.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Kessler, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yeah, it was a big development in the ongoing war in Bosnia-Herzegovina story, yes it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Even on a smaller level you said that it was often good to go to hospitals because they were a good place to find stories.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yep. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Stories, stories are a big thing for you in your profession, aren't they, Mr. Bowen?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Stories is what we refer to to the -- what we do, the events that we cover, we refer to them as stories. It doesn't mean to say they're not true. But we call them stories.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: But a story also has the implication of being somewhat sensational, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Doesn't it increase your chances of winning a prestigious award such as the Monte Carlo Award if the story you're covering has a somewhat sensational aspect to it?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I would hope that they don't award -- I would hope they don't give awards for sensationalism. I would say that a lot of the material that was in that film was dramatic and that's because we were covering very dramatic events and we were very close to them and we had very good access to them because we had pretty much free movement, considering there was a war going on in that part of Mostar at that particular time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: You said in answer to Mr. Karnavas that you wished that you had had the opportunity to present the other side by going to West Mostar, if I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I would have been delighted to have done another documentary even about that, but as I say when we asked to get the two- or three-week long access we needed, we weren't allowed to have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I take it from what you say that as a matter of principle you agree that it is important to present both sides of a story.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Of course it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Well, let me focus on one particular aspect of the story that was told in the documentary and that you've testified about today. You mentioned, and you've mentioned on previous occasions your belief that what was going on in -- in Mostar and generally with the Bosnian Croats was being done with some form of cooperation of the government of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And I want to talk with you for a moment about the basis for that opinion and what you did to verify it. Now, today is not the first time that you've testified under oath on that subject, is it?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I've testified in this court before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes. In the Tuta and Stela case you were asked questions about exactly that same subject?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And for the record, the matters that I'm going to mention to you are on page 5805 and page 5806 of the transcript from that case. Do you remember counsel for the Prosecution asking you what the basis was for your view that there was some cooperation by the government of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yeah, I do. Well, I saw the -- I had -- I looked through the transcript again yesterday, so, yes, I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: You do remember that. And let me -- let me remind you of one or two of the things that you said, if I could. You said when asked this question and I'm quoting now, "I can explain this on a number of different levels. There was evidence that I saw that there was an involvement by the Croatian army and, by extension, by the government in Zagreb." Do you remember giving that answer?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And then you went on to talk about having seen identity papers that had been taken from prisoners and dead bodies and so on.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: In addition to that, you also mentioned, as you did today, that you'd had a connection with -- a conversation with Dario Kordic.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I did indeed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And you've also said, as you have today, that you have spoken to people in Zagreb, and your expression then was -- on that occasion, "I also spoke to people in Zagreb, in an informal way, who told me about it."

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Karnavas mentioned another British journalist that we've heard of by the name of Belinda Giles. Is that somebody that you know?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I know Belinda, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Do you know a documentary programme that she produced for channel 4 in November of 1993 called, "A Greater Croatia"?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: So then you won't be aware that in the course of that documentary that -- that did deal in detail with the government of Croatia, Ms. Giles interviewed name of high-ranking people in the Croatian government?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I'm -- as I say, I didn't see the film so I'm not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: No knowledge about it. Sir, in preparing for your own documentary in which you made this allegation against the government of Croatia, did you interview any ministers of that government? ^^ ?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I had -- in the course of the previous two years of covering there I had been in Zagreb quite a few times, and I had interviewed a number of different people in the government, yes. I'd also had conversations with people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Let me -- let me put my question again. Perhaps I wasn't specific enough. For the purpose of making this documentary, did you interview anyone in the government of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: You did not. Did you interview anyone holding office in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: For this documentary, no, I didn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: You did not.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: -- for the reasons I've already given.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: By the way, I represent Mr. Bruno Stojic. Have you ever interviewed Bruno Stojic?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I haven't, no. I'm sure I would have remembered if I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Let me just ask you this, sir, then in -- in light of what you've just told us, is it your contention that this allegation that you make against the government of Croatia of being involved in a nationalist project, do you think that you have fairly presented both sides of that question? Sorry, I'm going to pause while the Judges confer for a moment. Let me repeat that question. Do you feel, based on what you've told us that in -- in making this allegation against the government of Croatia, you have fairly presented both sides of that question?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: The documentary was not about that particular question, but in the context of the wider story I mentioned it as a contributing factor. Had I wanted to do a documentary about that particular thing, then I would have gone into it in much more detail. But I was journalistically clear in my own mind based on those things that you've already discussed and that you've mentioned and read out from my previous testimony, I was clear in my own mind that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Based on --

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: And so were many other people at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Based upon the conversations you've told us about.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Conversations, yeah, in Bosnia. Conversations in Zagreb. Bloodstained identity papers that I was shown. There seemed to be a lot of indications. Plus as well, there were reports as -- it was something that was being reported at the time. It was part of the discourse at the time that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: It was part of the discourse; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes. Yeah it was part of the -- if you talked to people in Zagreb, it was almost --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bowen, to stay in line with the questioning by Mr. Murphy, I have the transcript of what you said in your documentary, and let me read this sentence to you. You're saying: "The Croatian propaganda is resounding across the lines in Mostar," and you add on to that, "Since May, Bosnian Croats aided and abetted by the Croatian government have been laying siege to about 60.000 people in East Mostar." When you say this as a journalist of the BBC, you must have imagined the impact your words would have. What allowed you at that moment to provide a comment to the effect of the Croatian government being involved in what was going on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Frankly, Your Honour, I didn't think me saying that at the time would come as a great surprise to anybody. It -- it had been, I think, quite widely reported already by other journalists. It was -- I think I used that phrase more as a reminder to what I hoped the audience had already picked up. I wasn't trying to break news to them at that particular point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So for you it was a notorious fact by then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was something that a lot of people talked about. You know, they'd say things like, "Well, how do you think the Bosnian Croats are continuing to be armed? Where do you think their weapons are coming from? Where do you think they get their -- the shells for their tanks from?" Even their uniforms. Their uniforms were -- even just the lowest level of circumstantial evidence let alone the other stuff. Their uniforms are almost identical to the uniforms of Croatian regulars. Their badges were almost identical. The -- as I say, I was a frequent visitor to Zagreb. I was a frequent visitor also to Split, and I had a lot of conversations about this kind of thing with people there, with people who were working in various capacities, officially and unofficially, working for the Croatian government. As I say, when I used that phrase in the script, I didn't think that would come as a surprise to anybody who would be following the story.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: So then, sir, you made the leap if I can put it in that way, from evidence of involvement by the Croatian army to evidence of a national project involving the Croatian government; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I had spent some time -- as I say, quite a lot of time in Croatia and I made the -- perhaps I never questioned the assumption, but I figured that the Croatian army was acting with the consent and under the direction of the president of Croatia, who was after all a former general.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: But you've never conducted interviews to verify that story, as far as we know?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I -- I had many off-the-record conversations on that story and I had an on-the-record interview with Dario Kordic in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Was Dario Kordic a member of the government of Croatia to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: No, but he was a senior are member of the leadership of Herceg-Bosna, and I felt that his opinion in that was therefore valid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Would Your Honour allow me just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Did you also become aware, sir, while you were making your research and investigating these questions of the presence of other foreign troops in Bosnia and Herzegovina during the war, some of them from Islamist countries?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yeah, I was aware of that. I heard that, for example, there were Afghans or -- anyway, some kind of Islamic forces around. Zenica particularly was well known as a centre for this kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Did you draw the conclusion from this that the government of Afghanistan was participating or encouraging some nationalist project in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Well, the government of Afghanistan was not a well-organised entity. I spent a lot of -- at that point I'd spent a lot of time in Afghanistan and in 1992 the Mujahedin overthrew the government of Afghanistan. So they were in no position to give orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Okay let's substitute Iran or Turkey or Syria. Take your pick. Now, did you draw the -- did you draw the inference, Mr. Bowen, that any of those governments was involved in a nationalist project in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I didn't know that there were Irans [sic], Turks, or Syrians who were said to be -- who were said to be there. The nationalities I heard were Afghans and Saudis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I have nothing further, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have only the Defence of Mr. Praljak, who will have 45 minutes given to them by Mrs. Tomic and Mr. Ibrisimovic. You have 45 minutes, which means we will have to continue tomorrow. Today we have 10 minutes. I give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]. Thank you, Your Honour. I will use the four minutes that the Prosecution has used on top of the time allocated to them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Bowen.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: During the time when you were in East Mostar, who was the commander of the HVO? During the time when you were in Mostar, who was the commander of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I was the commander of the HVO. My name is Praljak, and I'm one of the accused, and my question is this: Isn't it incredible for a professional BBC journalist not to know the name of the commander of the army that he talks so much about? Isn't that a very strange fact?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I did know your name because it was one of the names that people talked about.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, please. Mr. Bowen, please. I don't have much time, and that's why I would kindly ask you to answer me. From my CV, I can tell you that before the war I was a film director. I had authored a number of documentaries, and maybe we can talk on that level. So you don't know who the commander of the HVO was in -- during the time when you were in Mostar. Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Perhaps I didn't recall it, but I certainly knew your name, and perhaps at the time I knew that you were the commander. I think what I men in my answer was, if I did know, I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Kindly, let's refrain from "maybes." Let's try not to use too much "perhaps." We're dealing with facts here, so if you know something, tells us what you know. If you don't know, just say you don't know. I will move on to more important topics, but now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I think it is not feasible to ask a witness to state anything with certainty when a witness is in doubt because otherwise he would be lying. So I warn you not to make statements here that come close to inciting a witness to answer untruly. If the witness is insecure, he must honestly say "perhaps," or something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bowen, the question that Mr. Praljak is asking you, I would have asked you -- when you interviewed Mr. Arif Pasalic, and I would have thought you interviewed the commander of the 3rd Corps. Did it maybe occur to him to interview the other side, the commander of the other side? At the time it may have been difficult. However, at the time the commander of the HVO, did you know the name or did you not know the name of the HVO commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that the answer I gave a couple of minutes ago was frankly -- is probably a little ill thought out. I knew Mr. Praljak's name. I spoke in a lot of detail at the time about what was going on the time -- I spent a lot of time with Mr. Pasalic, and he spoke a lot about the people on the other side. So I -- I mean, I can't recall it recall it definitively, but I say I must have known his name because -- in fact, when I was asked about this particular case by a Croatian friend of mine and they said, who are the defendants, that was the first name that I came up with when I was reporting back to her what I was coming here to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're saying that Mr. Pasalic referred to some of the names of the people who were on the other side in the interview with yourself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Generals often talk about their opposite numbers. They are always interested in what they may or may not be doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Once again, please. Do you know who my deputy was, who was the deputy of the commander of the Main Staff of the HVO, who the deputy was?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Maybe I knew then. I can't recall now. If you tell me his name, I'll tell you if I recognise it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know who -- Mr. Pasalic was the commander of the 4th Corps. His counterpart on the HVO, there was something called that was called south-east Herzegovina Operation Zone. Do you know who the commander of that zone was, the zone of south-east Herzegovina which was at the same rank as Mr. Pasalic in the BH army?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I've got to admit I was not an expert on the order of battle of the HVO. Some of the individuals who were frequently talked about, and you were one of them, I was familiar with those names. Equally --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, you're stealing my time. You're wasting my time. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: May I answer your question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Please, do you know the name of the commander at the time of the south-east Herzegovina operations zone? You either know it or you don't. This is not matter of discussion.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: And I repeat perhaps I knew it then. I can't recall it now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. I have another minute. In the documentary, did you use only the material that you recorded in Mostar at the time, or did you also use some other materials? Please answer me as a professional, as one professional to another. Did you only use the material that you yourself recorded at the time or did you maybe use some materials that you didn't record or you recorded at some other time?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: We -- about -- of that 43 minutes, I would say about three minutes was taken from footage recorded during our first trip. Also while we were there we hired another guy and he was fully credited in the documentary to do additional camera work, someone called Nigel Chandler who was a British cameraman who was there. So effectively we had two cameras. So we used his material and our material. So effectively it was 100 per cent BBC material, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I didn't ask about BBC material. In your documentary, there is frame or maybe even a few frames which were recorded in the part of Mostar which was under the control of the HVO in Liskova Street. Is that correct? Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: That's not correct. Everything in our documentary came from the part that was under the control of the BiH. I forgot to say in what I was just telling you that we also had a few pictures which, if you remember, I mentioned in the soundtrack that were taken by a local man of the shelling of the -- of the old bridge.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, unfortunately it is 7.00, so we will continue tomorrow. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bowen, unfortunately you will have to spend the night in The Hague and return tomorrow afternoon. Unfortunately, again we sit in the afternoon, so you have to come back at quarter past 2.00. And it goes without saying that you should not talk to anybody about your testimony. You're now the witness of the justice since you have made a solemn declaration. I wish you a pleasant evening, and I invite you all to come back tomorrow at quarter past 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 24th day of January, 2007, at 2.15 p.m.
